e-tenses.whatItIs: Tests whether the verb form matches the time signal in the sentence and the sequence of other verbs around it. IBPS almost never asks 'name the tense' — tense appears buried inside error detection, cloze blanks, fillers and sentence improvement.
e-tenses.coreMethod:
1. Do NOT read the sentence for meaning first. SCAN for a time marker: since, for, ago, yesterday, last, by the time, already, just, yet, next, tomorrow, in <year>, when, before, after, until, no sooner, hardly, scarcely, it's high time.
2. Apply the marker-to-tense lock. These are fixed, not judgement calls:
   - since + POINT of time (2015, Monday, morning, he left) / for + PERIOD (two years, ages, a long time). Continuing action -> has been / have been + V-ing.
   - ago, yesterday, last night, in 1998 -> simple past ONLY. Present perfect with these is always wrong.
   - by the time + past clause -> past perfect in the other clause. 'By the time he arrived, the train HAD left.'
   - no sooner ... than / hardly ... when / scarcely ... before -> past perfect + simple past. 'No sooner HAD he sat down THAN the bell rang.'
   - it's high time / it's time / I wish / as if / as though / suppose -> V2 or 'were'. 'It is high time we LEFT' (not 'to go', not 'should go'). 'I wish I WERE rich.'
   - would rather / had better / rather than -> bare V1. 'I would rather GO.'
   - Conditional type 2: if + V2, would + V1. Type 3: if + had + V3, would have + V3. NEVER 'would' inside the if-clause.
   - After suggest / demand / insist / propose / recommend / order / urge / essential that / necessary that -> bare V1: 'He insisted that she GO.'
3. Sequence of tense: if the main verb is past, the subordinate verb goes past too — EXCEPT universal truths, which stay present. 'He said that the sun rises in the east' is correct.
4. Stative-verb check: know, believe, understand, belong, own, possess, contain, consist, seem, appear, resemble, hate, love, prefer, want, need, mean, matter do NOT take continuous forms. 'I am knowing the answer' is an error every time.
5. Auxiliary-form check: has/have/had + V3; is/am/are/was/were + V-ing or V3; did/does/do + V1; any modal + V1. A wrong participle after an auxiliary is the fastest tense error to spot.
6. If none of steps 2-5 trips, the tense is fine. Stop checking it and move to agreement or prepositions.
tricks: Read only the word AFTER since/for. Names a point (2015, Monday, childhood, he resigned) -> must be 'since'. Names a duration (two years, ages, a decade) -> must be 'for'. You never need the rest of the sentence.
'ago' + 'has/have' anywhere in the same clause is an automatic error. Mark it and move on without reading the sentence — saves 20 seconds.
Any sentence containing 'by the time', 'no sooner', 'hardly', 'scarcely' — jump straight to the two verbs. The error lives there roughly 80% of the time.

In cloze and fillers, first read the SURROUNDING sentences of the passage. If the passage narrates in past tense, delete every present-tense option instantly. This kills two of five options in one glance without any grammar reasoning.
'It is high time / It is time' is followed by V2. IBPS baits with 'It is high time we should go' and 'It is high time to go' — both wrong. Recognise the phrase as a shape, decide in 4 seconds.
Scan for stative verbs in -ing form (knowing, belonging, understanding, resembling, containing, seeming). These are visually obvious and are an instant error with no rule recall needed.
traps: Present perfect paired with a definite past adverb: 'He has submitted the form yesterday.' Aspirants read it as natural Indian English and pass over it.
Assuming 'since' always forces present perfect. 'I had been working there since 2010 before I resigned' is perfectly correct past perfect continuous — don't over-mark it.
'Since' meaning 'because' takes ANY tense. 'Since he is unwell, he will not attend' is fine. Decide which 'since' you are looking at before applying a rule.
Marking tense as the error when the verb form is right for the time but wrong for the SUBJECT — that is subject-verb agreement, a different part of the sentence and often a different labelled option.
'Would' inside the if-clause: 'If he would come, I would go.' Wrong. The if-clause never takes 'would' in exam grammar.
Reported speech: converting a universal truth to past. 'The teacher said that water boiled at 100 degrees' — the exam treats this as the error, not as acceptable.

Assuming a past-perfect-looking sentence needs past perfect. With plain 'before' and 'after', the sequence is already clear and simple past on both sides is acceptable — only mark it if the option set forces it.
e-tenses.timeTarget: 25-35 seconds per tense-based error-detection question once the marker table is automatic. 15 seconds for a tense-driven cloze or filler blank.
e-tenses.masteryCheck: Given 20 sentences each containing a time marker, you name the required tense in under 15 seconds each with 18/20 correct, without writing anything down and without re-reading the sentence.
questionPatterns: Error detection where a verb in one labelled part clashes with a time marker sitting in a different part.
Filler: 'He ______ in this bank since 2015.' Options: has worked / has been working / worked / had worked / is working.
Cloze blanks where all five options are the same verb in different tenses — the passage's surrounding tense is the only clue.
Sentence improvement where the underlined portion is the entire verb phrase.
Conditional-sentence errors: type 2 and type 3 mixed, or 'would' planted inside the if-clause.
Subjunctive after insist/demand/suggest/essential that — appears more at Mains than Prelims.
Reported-speech tense sequence, usually with a universal truth as the trap.

e-sva.whatItIs: Tests whether the verb matches its true subject in number. This is the single highest-frequency grammar rule in bank error detection — roughly one in three error-detection questions is built on it.
e-sva.coreMethod:
1. Find the main verb first, not the subject. Verbs are easier to spot (is/are/was/were/has/have/does/do or a word ending in -s).
2. Delete everything between the subject and that verb — every 'of' phrase, every relative clause, everything between two commas. Whatever noun survives is the subject. Internalise the reversal: -s on a NOUN means plural, -s on a VERB means singular.
3. Run the special-rule checklist in this order, fastest first:
   a. 'along with / as well as / together with / besides / in addition to / accompanied by / including / rather than / no less than / apart from' do NOT change the number. The subject is whatever came BEFORE them. 'The manager, along with his staff, IS attending.'
   b. Each / Every / Either / Neither / Everyone / Anyone / Someone / Nobody / Many a / More than one -> SINGULAR verb. 'Each of the students HAS submitted.'
   c. Either...or / Neither...nor / Not only...but also / or / nor -> verb agrees with the NEAREST subject. 'Neither the clerks nor the manager IS available.'
   d. Two nouns joined by 'and' -> plural. BUT singular when they name one person or one idea: 'The Collector and District Magistrate IS...', 'Bread and butter IS my breakfast', 'Slow and steady WINS the race'. If 'the' is repeated before the second noun, they are two things -> plural.
   e. 'A number of' + plural -> PLURAL verb. 'The number of' + plural -> SINGULAR verb. Memorise as a pair.
   f. Plural-looking but singular: news, mathematics, physics, economics, politics, ethics, statistics (the subject), measles, mumps, innings, summons, gallows, 'a means'.
   g. Singular-looking but plural: cattle, police, people, poultry, vermin, gentry, clergy, folk.
   h. Collective nouns (committee, government, jury, team, family, crowd, public, staff) -> singular by default in IBPS; plural only when the sentence stresses members acting separately.
   i. Amounts, distances and periods treated as one unit -> singular. 'Ten kilometres IS a long walk.' 'Five thousand rupees IS a large sum.'
   j. Fractions, percentages, some/most/half/all/rest/none + of + noun -> the verb follows the noun after 'of'. 'Half of the water IS gone.' 'Half of the students ARE absent.'
   k. 'One of the + plural noun + who/that' -> the verb after 'who' is PLURAL; the main verb agrees with 'One' and is singular. 'One of the officers who ARE eligible HAS applied.'
   l. There is / There are -> agrees with what FOLLOWS it.
4. Inversion check: after 'Never', 'Seldom', 'Not only', 'Hardly', 'Rarely' at the start of a sentence, the subject sits AFTER the auxiliary. Find it there before judging.
tricks: Cross out with your eyes everything from the first 'of' up to the verb, and everything sitting between two commas. What remains is the subject. This one move catches about 40% of all SVA errors in five seconds.

See 'along with / as well as / together with / including / accompanied by / besides / in addition to'? Stop. The subject is the word before it. This construction appears in nearly every IBPS paper because it works on so many candidates.
'A number of' = many = plural. 'The number of' = the count = singular. Two seconds, guaranteed appearance.

Work backwards, not forwards. Spot the auxiliary (is/are/was/were/has/have), then jump LEFT hunting for the subject. Reading the sentence forward wastes the first half of your time on words that don't matter.

In 'one of the + plural + who' constructions, the verb right after 'who' is plural. Aspirants instinctively 'correct' it to singular and lose the mark. Knowing this stops you re-checking a part that is already right.
If a sentence contains 'each' or 'every' before subjects joined by 'and', the verb is singular regardless: 'Every boy and every girl WAS present.'
In fillers where the five options differ only by is/are or has/have, do not read for meaning at all — locate the subject and answer in 10 seconds.
traps: 'The quality of the mangoes were not good.' The subject is 'quality' (singular). The plural noun sitting immediately before the verb is the entire trap and it works constantly.
Marking SVA when the real error is tense or pronoun in a different labelled part. Decide which rule the sentence is actually built on before committing.

'None of' — traditionally singular, but modern usage allows plural with plural nouns and IBPS usually accepts plural. Do not choose this part as the error unless nothing else in the sentence is wrong.
Inverted sentences: 'Never has such a thing been attempted' is correct. The auxiliary before the subject looks wrong to an untrained eye.
Plural-looking proper nouns: 'The United States IS', 'Gulliver's Travels IS', 'The Arabian Nights IS'.
'Many a' is singular despite meaning many: 'Many a man HAS tried and failed.'
Collective nouns: over-applying the 'plural when divided' rule. In IBPS the default answer is singular unless the sentence explicitly shows disagreement among members.
Forgetting that with either...or / neither...nor the verb follows the NEAREST subject, so reversing the order of the two nouns changes the correct verb.
e-sva.timeTarget: 20-30 seconds per SVA-based error question. This is the fastest error category to solve once the deletion move is automatic — treat anything over 35 seconds as a signal you have mis-identified the rule.
e-sva.masteryCheck: On a 10-question error-detection set built entirely on subject-verb agreement, you score 9/10 in under 4 minutes AND can name the specific rule (proximity, intervening phrase, collective noun, 'the number of', etc.) for every one you got right.
questionPatterns: Error detection with a long 'of' phrase or comma-inserted phrase between subject and verb.
Error detection using 'along with / as well as / together with' to disguise the subject.
'A number of' vs 'the number of' — appears almost every cycle.
Fillers where the five options differ only in is/are, has/have, was/were.
Sentence improvement where the underlined portion contains the verb and the subject sits outside it.
'One of the + plural noun + who' constructions, usually with the verb after 'who' as the tested spot.
Either...or / neither...nor proximity questions, sometimes with the singular noun placed second deliberately.
Cloze blanks where tense is obvious and only number distinguishes the options.

e-articles.whatItIs: Two small-word topics that together account for a quarter of all bank error-detection answers. Articles test whether a/an/the is present, absent or wrong; prepositions are mostly fixed collocations to be recalled, not reasoned out.
e-articles.coreMethod:
ARTICLES:
1. a/an goes by SOUND, not spelling. 'A' before consonant sounds: a university, a European, a one-rupee note, a unique case, a useful tool, a habit. 'An' before vowel sounds: an hour, an honest man, an heir, an honour, an MP, an MLA, an FIR, an SP, an X-ray, an 8-year-old.
2. 'The' is REQUIRED with: superlatives (the best), ordinals (the first), unique objects (the sun, the earth), rivers/seas/oceans/mountain ranges/deserts/island groups (the Ganga, the Himalayas, the Thar), plural country names (the Netherlands, the USA, the Philippines), newspapers, holy books, musical instruments (play the flute), an adjective used as a class noun (the poor, the rich), 'the more...the merrier' pairs, directions (the north), and any noun already introduced.
3. 'The' is NOT used with: languages (He speaks English), meals (had lunch), games (play cricket), abstract nouns in general sense (Honesty is the best policy), plural nouns in general sense (Books are my friends), single mountains (Mount Everest), diseases, and go to school/college/church/bed/hospital/prison when named for their purpose.
4. Every singular countable noun needs SOME determiner. 'He is doctor' is an error; 'He is a doctor' is right. Scan for bare singular countables.

PREPOSITIONS:
1. Do not reason about meaning. Identify the word immediately governing the preposition — the verb, adjective or noun before it — and recall its fixed partner.
2. Check first for verbs that take NO preposition but that Indian usage adds one to. This is the highest-yield check in the whole topic: discuss, describe, marry, resemble, reach, order, request, attack, accompany, enter, join, sign, comprise, resign, emphasise, investigate, ridicule, board, lack, await, approach, precede. 'Discuss about the matter' is the most-repeated preposition error in Indian bank exams.
3. Then check the high-frequency fixed pairs: accuse OF, charge WITH, blame FOR (blame something ON someone), afraid/ashamed/aware/capable/confident/guilty/proud/suspicious/jealous OF, angry WITH a person but angry AT a thing, comply WITH, conform TO, deal IN goods but deal WITH a person, die OF a disease / FROM a cause / BY violence / FOR a cause, differ WITH a person but differ FROM in nature, prefer X TO Y, superior/inferior/senior/junior/prior/preferable TO, consist OF, composed OF, insist ON, depend ON, rely ON, congratulate ON, concentrate ON, familiar WITH a thing but familiar TO a person, married TO, key/solution/answer/clue/access/exception TO, devoid OF, abide BY, adhere TO, apologise TO someone FOR something, succeed IN, result IN an outcome but result FROM a cause, part WITH a thing but part FROM a person, in charge OF, on behalf OF.
4. Then time and place: in (months, years, seasons, cities, enclosed spaces), on (days, dates, surfaces, streets), at (clock times, precise points, small places), by (a deadline), till/until (up to a time), since (a point), for (a period), from...to (a span).
tricks: 'prefer / senior / junior / superior / inferior / prior / preferable' followed by 'than' IS the error. Six words, zero further reading, 20 seconds saved every time it appears — and it appears often.

Scan for discuss / describe / reach / marry / resemble / enter / join / order / request / attack / accompany followed by any preposition. The preposition itself is the answer. Do this scan before reading the sentence for meaning.
For a/an, say the word silently and judge the first SOUND. 'An university' fails the sound test in half a second without any rule recall.
A superlative or 'most' without 'the' is an instant error. Visually scan for -est endings and the word 'most'. 'He is best player in the team' — mark and move.
'One of the' must be followed by a PLURAL noun. 'One of the reason' is an error every single time. This shape appears in almost every paper and takes two seconds to catch.
In double-filler and cloze questions, settle the PREPOSITION before you consider meaning. Prepositions are binary — right or wrong — while meaning is arguable, so they eliminate options faster.

Build one card of only the ~30 verb+preposition pairs you personally get wrong, not the textbook list of 200. Revising 30 pairs daily for two weeks makes them automatic; revising 200 makes none of them automatic.
traps: Uncountable nouns taking 'a/an' or a plural -s: an advice, informations, furnitures, equipments, luggages, machineries, evidences, sceneries, stationeries, knowledges, works (in the sense of labour). The fix is usually DELETING the article, not swapping it.
Marking 'the' before a proper noun as wrong when the noun has been made specific: 'the India of my dreams', 'the Mahatma Gandhi of our times' are both correct.
Over-marking idiomatic prepositions that are correct but sound unusual. If you cannot name the governing collocation, do not mark it as the error.

'Between' for two, 'among' for more than two — but 'between' is legitimate for more than two when relationships are individual and mutual ('an agreement between five banks'). Don't reflexively mark it.

'Good in English' (should be good AT), 'different than' (should be different FROM), 'cope up with' (should be cope WITH), 'comprises of' (comprise takes nothing), 'married with' (should be married TO), 'revert back', 'order for' — these read as normal Indian English and slip past on the first read.
Confusing an article error with a noun-number error inside the same phrase. Check which labelled part boundary the error actually falls in before choosing.
'In' vs 'into' for motion: IBPS still tests 'jumped INTO the river' even though 'in' is widely accepted in speech.
e-articles.timeTarget: Article errors: 15-20 seconds. Preposition errors: 25-30 seconds when the collocation is known. If you do not know the collocation within 30 seconds, you will not derive it — skip.
e-articles.masteryCheck: You can write out the 30 highest-frequency verb-and-adjective preposition pairs from memory with 27+ correct, and on a 15-question mixed article-and-preposition set you score 13+ in under 6 minutes.
questionPatterns: Error detection where a short labelled part contains only 'a/an/the' plus a noun — the shortest parts are the favourite hiding place.
Error detection where a common verb is followed by a wrongly added preposition (discuss about, reach at, marry with).
'Prefer ... than' and 'senior/superior ... than' constructions.
Single and double fillers where the options differ only in the preposition.
Cloze blanks where the missing word is a preposition inside a phrasal verb.
Sentence improvement where the underlined phrase is a preposition-plus-noun chunk.
Missing article before a singular countable noun, or a superlative with no 'the'.
'One of the + singular noun' — an article/noun hybrid that appears constantly.

e-noun.whatItIs: Tests noun countability and number, and pronoun case and agreement. The errors are small-word errors, which means they are easy to miss on a fast read and quick to confirm once you know where to look.
e-noun.coreMethod:
NOUNS:
1. Countability check on every noun. Uncountables take no plural -s and no a/an: advice, information, luggage, baggage, furniture, equipment, machinery, scenery, poetry, stationery, evidence, knowledge, news, work, bread, money, traffic, weather, jewellery, offspring. They take much/little/a great deal of/an amount of — never many/few/a number of.
2. Nouns always plural (no singular form, plural verb): scissors, trousers, spectacles, tongs, pliers, shorts, jeans, premises, thanks, riches, alms, amends, arrears, belongings, surroundings, valuables, savings, proceeds, outskirts, particulars, wages.
3. Nouns plural in form but singular in meaning: news, mathematics, physics, economics, ethics, politics, statistics (the subject), innings, summons, measles, mumps, billiards.
4. After a NUMBER, these stay singular: 'a ten-rupee note', 'a five-year plan', 'two dozen eggs', 'five hundred men', 'three score'. They take -s only when indefinite and followed by 'of': 'dozens of', 'hundreds of', 'scores of'.
5. Possessive: apostrophe with living things, personified nouns and time/measure expressions ('a day's work', 'two weeks' notice', 'a stone's throw', 'the earth's surface'). Use 'of' with inanimate objects ('the leg of the table').
6. Countable/uncountable quantifier match: 'less' + uncountable, 'fewer' + countable. 'Less students' is an error. 'Amount of people' is an error (should be 'number of').

PRONOUNS:
1. Case: subjective (I, he, she, we, they, who) as subject; objective (me, him, her, us, them, whom) after every preposition and as every object. 'Between you and I' is wrong — 'between you and me'. Test who/whom by substituting he/him: he -> who, him -> whom.
2. After 'than' or 'as' in a comparison, use the case the pronoun would take if the verb were completed: 'He is taller than I (am).'
3. 'Let' takes the objective case: 'Let him and me go.'
4. Order of pronouns: 231 normally (You, he and I); 123 when admitting a fault (I, you and he are to blame).
5. Reflexives (myself, himself) only when subject and object are the same person, or for emphasis. 'Myself Rahul' is wrong. Verbs NOT followed by a reflexive: keep, stop, qualify, bathe, hide, move, rest, turn, feel. Verbs that DO take one: absent, avail, pride, resign, acquaint, adapt, apply, exert, enjoy (when reflexive sense intended).
6. Antecedent agreement: each/every/everyone/everybody/anyone/nobody/either/neither are singular and take his/her/its, not their, in exam grammar. 'Each of the boys did HIS work.'
7. 'One' must be followed by one's/oneself, never his/himself: 'One must do one's duty.'
8. Relative pronouns: 'that' only in defining clauses and never after a preposition ('the man to whom I spoke', not 'to that'); 'which' for things; 'who/whom' for people; after a comma use who/which, never that.
tricks: Scan for three specific spots where pronoun-case errors are planted: 'between you and ___', 'let ___ and ___', and '___ than ___'. Checking only these three shapes catches most pronoun-case items in ten seconds.
Any pronoun immediately after a preposition must be objective. 'for he', 'to she', 'with I', 'between he and I' — that IS the error, stop reading the rest of the sentence.

If the sentence contains each / every / everyone / everybody / anyone / nobody / either / neither and later uses their/them/they, that is a pronoun-agreement error in exam grammar. Two-word scan, no parsing.
If a sentence begins with 'One', every subsequent pronoun must be one's or oneself. A single 'his' or 'himself' anywhere after it is the error.

Scan every noun ending in -s for the uncountables: informations, equipments, furnitures, luggages, advices, machineries, evidences, sceneries, stationeries. Purely visual, two seconds, and one of these appears in most papers.
Check 'less/fewer' and 'amount/number' against the noun that follows. 'Less students', 'amount of people', 'number of water' are instant errors requiring no sentence comprehension.
traps: Over-correcting who/whom. Apply the he/him substitution rather than guessing that 'whom' sounds more formal and therefore more correct.
'Each other' for two and 'one another' for more than two is the textbook rule, but modern usage blurs it and IBPS rarely makes it the answer. Only choose it if nothing else in the sentence is wrong.
'Hundreds of people' is correct; 'two hundreds people' is wrong. The -s appears only when no number precedes it.
Assuming 'people' is always plural — 'peoples' is correct when it means nations or ethnic groups.
Marking a valid time-or-measure possessive as an error: 'two weeks' notice', 'a day's journey', 'ten rupees' worth' are all correct.
Confusing a noun-number error with an article error in the same phrase. Identify which labelled part boundary the fault actually falls inside.
'Myself/himself' used for emphasis is correct: 'I myself saw it.' Only the wrong-subject use is an error.

e-adjective.whatItIs: Tests degree of comparison, the adjective-versus-adverb choice after linking verbs, and word placement. Most of these errors are visually identifiable — you can spot them without parsing the sentence, which makes this the fastest-scoring grammar topic in the section.
e-adjective.coreMethod:
1. Adjective modifies a noun or pronoun; adverb modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb. Quick test: if the word answers HOW an action was performed, it must be an adverb.
2. LINKING-VERB RULE. After be, seem, appear, look, feel, taste, smell, sound, become, grow, turn, remain, keep, prove — use an ADJECTIVE. 'The soup tastes good' (not 'well'). 'He looks sad' (not 'sadly'). But when the same verb is used actively, the adverb is right: 'He looked at me sadly.'
3. DEGREE RULES:
   - Two things -> comparative + 'than'. More than two -> superlative + 'the'.
   - Double comparatives and superlatives are errors: 'more better', 'most easiest', 'more superior', 'most fastest'.
   - Latin comparatives take TO, never THAN: superior, inferior, senior, junior, prior, posterior, anterior, preferable.
   - Absolute adjectives cannot be compared: unique, perfect, complete, universal, ideal, entire, extreme, chief, full, empty, round, square, eternal, infinite, supreme. 'More unique' and 'most perfect' are errors.
   - Comparing within the same class needs 'than any OTHER + singular': 'Delhi is bigger than any other city in India.' Comparing across classes drops 'other': 'Delhi is bigger than any city in Sri Lanka.'
   - 'The + comparative, the + comparative': 'The higher you climb, the colder it gets.'
4. ADVERB PLACEMENT. only, even, also, merely, nearly, almost, hardly, scarcely must sit immediately before the word they modify. 'He only bought two books' vs 'He bought only two books' — different meanings, and misplacement is a favourite IBPS trap in sentence improvement.
5. DOUBLE NEGATIVES. hardly, scarcely, barely, seldom, rarely are already negative. Adding not/no/never/nothing is an error. Also fix the partners: hardly/scarcely/barely ... WHEN or BEFORE (never 'than'); no sooner ... THAN (never 'when').
6. VERY vs MUCH. 'Very' modifies the positive degree and present participles; 'much' modifies comparatives and past participles. 'Very tired' but 'much better', 'much surprised', 'much annoyed'.
7. 'Enough' FOLLOWS the word it modifies: 'good enough', 'fast enough' — never 'enough good'.
8. CONFUSABLE PAIRS that are not simply adjective/adverb versions of each other: late/lately, hard/hardly, near/nearly, high/highly, most/mostly, short/shortly, fair/fairly, just/justly, deep/deeply, sure/surely. 'He works hard' vs 'He hardly works' are opposite in meaning.
tricks: Scan for an -ly word sitting next to a linking verb (tastes, smells, looks, feels, sounds, seems, appears). That is an instant error requiring no comprehension. 'The flowers smell sweetly' — mark and move in five seconds.

Scan for 'more' or 'most' placed in front of a word already ending in -er/-est, or in front of an absolute adjective (unique, perfect, complete, superior, ideal). Purely visual detection, under ten seconds, and one of the most repeated IBPS shapes.

'superior / inferior / senior / junior / prior / preferable' followed by 'than' is always the error. Same shape as the preposition rule — worth double-checking for because it appears in both topic areas.
'than any' in a same-class comparison with 'other' missing is the error. Check whether the two things being compared belong to the same group; if yes, 'other' must be there.
If a sentence contains hardly / scarcely / seldom / rarely / barely AND a not / no / nothing / never, it is a double-negative error. Two-word visual scan, no parsing.

In sentence improvement, if the underlined portion contains 'only' or 'even', the question is almost certainly about placement, not grammar. Ask where the restriction logically belongs and pick that option directly.
traps: 'I feel well' is CORRECT — 'well' is also an adjective meaning healthy. The genuinely tested pair is 'I feel bad' (correct) versus 'I feel badly' (wrong).
'Elder' is used only for family members, only before the noun, and never with 'than'. 'My elder brother' is right; 'elder than me' is wrong; 'older than me' is right.
'Farther' is physical distance, 'further' is additional. 'Latest' is most recent, 'last' is final. Both pairs appear occasionally and both are easy to over-mark.
Inversion after a negative opener is CORRECT and looks wrong: 'Seldom does he come late', 'Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang.' Do not mark the word order as the error.
Over-applying the absolute-adjective rule. IBPS treats 'more unique' as an error, but do not extend the rule to adjectives that are merely strong (e.g. 'more essential' is acceptable).
Confusing an adverb error with a phrasal-verb particle. In 'He put off the meeting', 'off' is part of the verb, not a misplaced adverb.
Marking 'much' or 'very' wrong when the participle is functioning as a plain adjective: 'very tired' and 'very interested' are both correct despite being past participles in origin.

e-adjective.masteryCheck: On 20 sentences each containing one adjective or adverb error, you score 17+ at an average under 25 seconds, and you can list all 14 absolute adjectives and all 7 Latin comparatives from memory.

e-rc-technique.whatItIs: The procedure for extracting 8-10 answers from a 350-450 word passage inside 6 minutes. RC is about 9 of 30 Prelims English questions and appears in every shift, so this method is the single most valuable thing in the section.
e-rc-technique.coreMethod:
THE PRELIMS METHOD — question-first, targeted scan. Total budget for a 9-question set: 6 minutes.

STEP 1 (20 seconds) — Read only the QUESTION STEMS. Not the options. Classify each stem as: VOCAB (synonym/antonym of a highlighted word) / DETAIL ('according to the passage') / INFERENCE ('can be inferred', 'the author implies') / THEME or TITLE / TONE / multi-statement (I, II, III). You now know what you are hunting for before you read a word of the passage.

STEP 2 (2 to 2.5 minutes) — Read the passage exactly ONCE at normal speed, doing only three things:
  (a) Mark the sentence carrying the main claim. In bank RC it is usually the last sentence of paragraph 1 or the first sentence of paragraph 2.
  (b) Circle every contrast connector: but, however, although, despite, nevertheless, yet, while, whereas, on the contrary. Inference answers cluster around these.
  (c) Circle every number, year, name and proper noun. Detail questions are built on these.
Do not try to understand every sentence. Do not stop for unknown words. Do not re-read.

STEP 3 — Answer in THIS order, ignoring the printed order:
  (i) VOCAB first — 15-20 seconds each. Go to the highlighted word, read its sentence plus the one before, pick the option that can physically replace the word in that sentence.
  (ii) DETAIL next — 30-40 seconds each. Take the keyword from the stem, scan for it in the passage, read two sentences around it. Never answer from memory of your read.
  (iii) THEME/TITLE — you already marked the main claim in step 2.
  (iv) TONE.
  (v) INFERENCE last, and only if the clock allows.

STEP 4 — For 'which of the following is TRUE / NOT TRUE / EXCEPT' with three or five statements: verify each statement individually against the text, marking T or F on your rough sheet. Do not eliminate options directly; you will end up re-reading.

STEP 5 — HARD SKIP RULE. If 45 seconds on one question has not narrowed you to two options, mark it and leave. Under a 20-minute sectional clock, one stubborn RC question costs you two easy grammar questions elsewhere.

THE EXCEPTION: question-first works for Prelims-length passages and short Mains sets. For Mains LONG passages (600+ words, 8-10 questions), switch to passage-first with paragraph tagging — see the Mains RC topic.
tricks: Read the question STEMS first, but never the OPTIONS first. Options are written to be plausible; reading five options before you know the passage plants wrong ideas in your head and roughly doubles your time per question.

Do vocabulary sub-questions WITHOUT reading the passage at all when short on time. Find the highlighted word, read only its sentence. Fifteen seconds each at near-perfect accuracy. A typical 9-question set has 2-3 of these — three nearly free marks even if you abandon the rest of the set.

For NOT-TRUE and EXCEPT questions, verify the three options you can confirm as TRUE; the leftover is the answer. Hunting directly for the false statement is measurably slower because false statements are written to look plausible.

Extreme-language elimination: in inference questions, options containing all, never, only, always, none, completely, entirely, must are wrong far more often than not, because passages hedge. Cross these first, before reading for meaning.
The correct inference option is usually a PARAPHRASE. If an option repeats passage wording verbatim, be suspicious — verbatim options are usually distorted by one changed word.

For TONE, ignore the topic entirely and look only at the author's adjectives and verbs. Emotive negatives (unfortunately, alarming, failed, neglected, dismal) -> critical. Neutral reporting verbs -> analytical or objective. Two-thirds of bank tone answers are analytical, critical, objective/neutral, or optimistic. Sarcastic, cynical, caustic, vindictive and apathetic are almost never correct for an editorial-style passage.
For TITLE questions, eliminate any title that names something appearing in only ONE paragraph. The correct title always covers the whole passage.
Detail-question answers usually follow passage order. If Q2's answer was in paragraph 1, Q3's is in paragraph 1 or 2. Never scan from the top again.
If after 40 seconds of reading you cannot follow the passage at all, abandon the set. There are 21 non-RC questions in Prelims English. RC is not compulsory.
traps: Answering from prior knowledge or real-world truth rather than the passage. This is the single biggest RC mark-loser at Clerk level, and it feels like confidence while it is happening.
Reading the passage twice. If you have read it twice you have already lost the set on time, whatever your accuracy.
Stopping on an unknown word mid-passage. Skip it — the meaning is usually recoverable from the sentence, and you may never need it.
Choosing an option that is TRUE in the world but not STATED in the passage. Every correct answer must be traceable to a specific line.
Half-right options: the first clause matches the passage and the second contradicts it. Read every option all the way to the end before selecting.
Right fact, wrong question — the option states something the passage genuinely says, but it does not answer the stem that was asked.
Assuming the conclusion is in the last paragraph. In editorial-style bank passages the thesis is often in paragraph 1 or 2, and the last paragraph is a recommendation, not the main claim.
Doing RC first in Prelims out of habit. It is high-mark but unbounded in time cost — see the section strategy for where it actually belongs.
Treating a 'according to the passage' question as an inference question and over-thinking it. Detail questions have literal answers sitting in the text.

e-rc-econ.topicName: RC on economic and banking themes
e-rc-econ.whatItIs: RC passages drawn from editorials on monetary policy, inflation, banking regulation, NPAs, fiscal deficit, digital payments and financial inclusion. A distinct topic because the vocabulary is a closed set and the argument structures repeat — which means these passages can be made your fastest, not your hardest.
e-rc-econ.coreMethod:
1. PRE-LOAD THE LEXICON. Roughly 120 terms cover 90% of these passages. Learn them before the exam so you never spend reading time decoding: inflation, deflation, disinflation, stagflation, repo rate, reverse repo, liquidity, monetary tightening/easing, fiscal deficit, revenue deficit, NPA, bad loan, haircut, provisioning, recapitalisation, moratorium, disbursement, credit offtake, CASA, capital adequacy, systemic risk, moral hazard, subsidy, austerity, stimulus, GDP, GVA, current account deficit, FDI, FII, depreciation, tariff, protectionism, demand-side, supply-side, capex, informal sector, financial inclusion, microfinance, insolvency, IBC, securitisation, yield, bond, benchmark, MCLR, priority sector lending, disintermediation, arbitrage, volatility, headwinds, tailwinds.
2. NAME THE ARGUMENT SHAPE in the first 30 seconds. In practice there are only five: (a) problem -> cause -> consequence -> recommendation; (b) policy announced -> benefits claimed -> limitations; (c) two-sided debate -> author leans one way at the end; (d) data/trend -> explanation -> outlook; (e) historical comparison -> present situation -> lesson. Once you have named the shape you know exactly where the central-idea and author's-view answers sit.
3. LOCATE THE AUTHOR'S OPINION. In economic editorials it is almost always in the final paragraph, or in the sentence immediately after the first strong contrast word. Mark that sentence during your single read.
4. DETAIL QUESTIONS here are usually cause-effect ('what, according to the author, is the reason for X'). Find X in the passage, then read the sentence BEFORE it — in this register the cause almost always precedes the effect.
5. TREAT NUMBERS AS LANDMARKS, NOT DATA. Statistics in these passages are decoration about 80% of the time. Circle where they are so you can jump back, but do not read them carefully and never do arithmetic.
6. TRACK WHO IS SPEAKING. These passages quote critics, economists, the RBI, the government and industry. Every time you see 'critics argue', 'the government claims', 'economists warn', put a small mark. Author's-view questions are built on candidates confusing a quoted view with the author's.
tricks: Read one editorial a day from The Hindu business page, Business Standard, Livemint or the Indian Express 'Explained' section. The point is not vague English improvement — it is that the vocabulary becomes automatic, which turns a 4-minute passage into a 2-minute one. That is the entire return on the habit.
Keep a one-page 'econ RC glossary' of only the terms that actually slowed you down. After about 30 days it stops growing. That plateau is your proof the habit has done its job.
The sentence after the FIRST 'however' in an economic editorial is very often the thesis. Read that one sentence twice and the rest once.

For 'the author's attitude towards <policy>', read only the modal verbs: 'must', 'should', 'needs to' signal advocacy; 'may', 'might', 'appears', 'could' signal hedging; 'failed to', 'little more than', 'at best', 'falls short' signal criticism. You can answer a tone question from modals alone in 20 seconds.

Reject any option that upgrades a correlation into a causation. If the passage says two things 'are associated with' or 'coincided with' each other and the option says one 'causes' the other, that option is wrong. This single check resolves a large share of economic-RC inference questions.

Because the vocabulary is closed, economic passages should become your FASTEST RC type within six weeks of daily editorial reading. If they are still your slowest after that, the glossary habit is not being done properly.
traps: Using your General Awareness knowledge to answer. You may know the current repo rate; the passage may be from three years ago. Every answer must come from the text.
Confusing a critic's argument with the author's position. Economic editorials quote opponents at length, and 'Critics argue that...' is not the author's view.

Assuming a negative-sounding passage means the author opposes the policy. Very often the author supports it and is listing risks — the tone question then has 'cautiously supportive' or 'analytical' as the answer, not 'critical'.
Getting bogged down in a statistics-heavy paragraph. Skim it; the questions rarely require the numbers.
Mistaking a recommendation for a fact: 'the government should recapitalise the banks' is not the same as 'the government recapitalised the banks', and detail questions exploit exactly this gap.
Picking the technically correct economics answer over the one the passage states. Your knowledge is a reading-speed advantage, never an answering shortcut.
Assuming every economic passage is anti-government or pro-reform. The stance varies by source and the tone question punishes assumptions.
e-rc-econ.timeTarget: Prelims set (400 words, 8-9 questions): 5.5 to 6.5 minutes. Mains set (600-700 words, 10 questions): 8 to 9 minutes. Once the lexicon is automatic these should run 30 to 60 seconds faster than an equivalent social-theme passage.

Test this by writing the two sentences down, then re-reading the editorial to check you were right.

'What, according to the author, is the primary reason for <the problem>?' — cause-effect detail.
'Which of the following would the author most likely support?' — author's view, answered from the final paragraph.
'What does the author imply about <the policy>?' — inference built on a contrast connector.
Tone: analytical, critical, cautiously optimistic, objective, concerned.
Synonym/antonym of a highlighted economic or general term used in a specific sense.
'Which of the following statements is NOT true according to the passage' with three statements built from different paragraphs.
Occasionally a question distinguishing the author's view from a quoted critic's view.

e-rc-social.whatItIs: Passages on education, gender, health, environment, urbanisation, migration, inequality, technology-and-society, mental health and employment. More abstract vocabulary, longer sentences and a heavier inference load than economic passages — and at Clerk level this is also where narrative and story-based passages appear.
e-rc-social.coreMethod:
1. SEPARATE CLAIM FROM EVIDENCE. Social passages are claim-driven rather than data-driven. As you read, keep two things distinct: the CLAIM (a 'should', 'must' or 'is failing' sentence) and the EVIDENCE (anecdotes, examples, studies). Nearly every inference question in a social passage tests whether you can tell them apart.
2. USE PARAGRAPH OPENERS AS A MAP. Social-theme passages are more likely than economic ones to be organised one-idea-per-paragraph, so the first sentence of each paragraph is a reliable index. Read those sentences with extra attention on your single pass.
3. HANDLE ABSTRACT WORDS BY READING FORWARD, NOT STOPPING. When you hit a term you do not know (stigma, precarity, hegemony, marginalisation, agency), do not stop. Social writing almost always restates or exemplifies the abstract term in the very next sentence. Read on and the meaning arrives free.
4. FOR NARRATIVE PASSAGES (common at Clerk level, rare at PO level), track four things only: who, what changed, why it changed, and what the point of the story is. Questions are mostly detail plus 'what does the passage suggest about the character'. Do not look for a thesis — narrative passages have a moral, not an argument.
5. LONG-SENTENCE DISCIPLINE. These passages use 35-45 word sentences with multiple clauses. Read to the first full stop, then name the subject and the main verb in your head before continuing. If you cannot name them, re-read that one sentence — not the paragraph.
6. ATTACK ORDER: vocabulary -> detail -> theme -> tone -> inference. Same order as general RC, but budget more time for inference here, because social passages typically carry 2-3 inference questions rather than 1.
tricks: Social passages hedge heavily, so hedged options win. In inference questions, options containing 'may', 'often', 'tends to', 'in some cases', 'can' are more likely correct, and absolutes ('all', 'never', 'always', 'none') more likely wrong. This signal is stronger in social passages than in economic ones.

Check every option for the quantifier switch. If the passage says 'many women' or 'some migrants' and the option says 'women' or 'all migrants', that single-word generalisation is the most common wrong-option construction in social RC. Scanning options for this alone catches several marks per paper.
For 'the author would most likely agree with', pick the option that restates the passage's central claim in WEAKER language. Correct answers are almost never stronger than the passage itself.

Tone options for social passages cluster in a small set: concerned, critical, sympathetic, analytical, objective. If the author uses emotive language about people affected -> sympathetic or concerned. If about institutions or policy -> critical. Twenty seconds, decided from adjectives alone.

The opening anecdote is never the thesis. In social passages the story is an illustration and the actual claim arrives one or two paragraphs later — go looking for it there when a central-idea question appears.

Read The Hindu op-eds and Indian Express editorials on social subjects specifically. Bank RC passages copy this exact sentence architecture, so familiarity with the register translates directly into reading speed.
traps: Moralising — picking the option that sounds most socially virtuous rather than the one the passage actually states. Option-writers exploit this deliberately and it is the defining trap of social RC.
Answering a 'what does the author suggest' question with your own opinion on the social issue. You have opinions about education and gender; the passage may not share them.
Anecdote-as-thesis: treating the opening story as the main idea and choosing a title based on it.
Losing the subject of a long multi-clause sentence by the time you reach the verb, then answering from a half-parsed sentence.
Assuming that criticism of a policy means opposition to the goal. An author can support universal education and criticise how it is being delivered — and the tone question hinges on that distinction.
Treating a narrative passage like an argumentative one and hunting for a thesis that does not exist.
Over-reading inference questions. Even in social passages the correct inference is one small step from the text, never two.

Skipping social passages because the vocabulary looks harder. The vocabulary is more abstract but the logic is simpler than in economic passages — the questions are usually more directly traceable to lines.
e-rc-social.timeTarget: Prelims set (400 words, 8-9 questions): 6 to 7 minutes — expect this to run 30 seconds slower than an economic set because of the extra inference questions. Mains set (600-700 words): 8.5 to 9.5 minutes. Inference questions here: 50-60 seconds each.
e-rc-social.masteryCheck: On a fresh social-theme passage with 8 questions including 3 inference questions, you score 6 or more in under 7 minutes, and on every inference question you got right you can point to the specific line the inference was one step away from.
questionPatterns: Central idea or title, where the opening anecdote is planted as a decoy title.
'What can be inferred about <the group discussed>?' — usually 2 of these per set.
Detail questions on a study, survey or example mentioned in the passage.
'The author's attitude towards <the institution/policy> is best described as...' — tone.
'Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a reason for <the problem>?'
Synonym or antonym of an abstract highlighted word used in a specific sense.
'What does the passage suggest about the character/protagonist?' — for narrative passages.
Multi-statement questions where one statement over-generalises what the passage said about 'some' or 'many'.

e-rc-long.whatItIs: A 600-800 word passage with 8-10 questions in the Mains paper, where English is 40 questions in 35 minutes and every mark counts toward the final merit list. RC is about 13 of those 40 marks, so this cannot be skipped the way a Prelims set can.
e-rc-long.coreMethod:
1. BUDGET. 9 minutes for a 10-question long set — about 54 seconds per question, of which the passage itself consumes 3.5 to 4 minutes. Set this cap before you start and honour it.
2. READ THE PASSAGE FIRST, NOT THE QUESTIONS. This is the opposite of the Prelims rule and it matters. With 700 words and 8-10 questions, reading stems first costs more than it saves, and the theme, tone and inference questions all require a whole-passage view anyway.
3. PARAGRAPH TAGGING — the core technique. After each paragraph, write a 2-3 word label in the margin: 'P1: the problem', 'P2: RBI response', 'P3: critique', 'P4: what next'. Five seconds per paragraph, and it saves 60+ seconds on every subsequent detail question because you jump straight to the right paragraph instead of scanning 700 words. This is the highest-return habit in Mains English.
4. ORDER OF ATTEMPT within the set: vocabulary -> detail (jump using your tags) -> central idea -> tone -> inference -> multi-statement questions LAST. Multi-statement items are the most time-expensive per mark in the entire paper.
5. MULTI-STATEMENT HANDLING (I/II/III, 'which of the following is/are true'): evaluate each statement independently against its tagged paragraph, write T or F for each on the rough sheet, and only then look at the options. Never eliminate options directly — you will end up re-reading the passage.
6. DETAIL-QUESTION ORDERING. In Mains long passages, detail questions follow passage order roughly 70% of the time. If Q3's answer came from paragraph 2, start Q4 in paragraph 2 or 3. Never restart from the top.
7. TRIAGE BETWEEN SETS. If the Mains paper has two RC sets and one passage is opaque after paragraph 1, do the other set first and return. The whole 35 minutes is yours to allocate within English — there is no sub-sectional lock.
8. ABANDON RULE. Hard cap of 10 minutes on a single long set. At 10 minutes, answer what you have, mark the rest, and move on. Twelve minutes on one RC set is how candidates leave 15 questions unattempted.
tricks: Paragraph tagging is the trick. Nothing else in Mains RC returns as much time. Practise it until the labels appear without conscious effort — five words per paragraph, no full sentences.

Go directly to the last paragraph for any 'the author's conclusion/suggestion/recommendation is' question. In long editorial passages this answer is in the final paragraph well over half the time, and you do not need to recall anything.

For highlighted-word vocabulary questions at Mains (which often test a secondary meaning), substitute each option into the ORIGINAL sentence and read it mentally. Wrong options usually break the grammar or the register even when the dictionary meaning seems close — much faster than trying to recall definitions.

For 'which of the following would weaken/strengthen the author's argument', pick the option that attacks the CAUSAL LINK, not the one that simply disagrees with the conclusion. Options that merely contradict the conclusion are the standard decoy.
Use the contrast connectors as a tagging shortcut. If a paragraph opens with 'However' or 'Yet', tag it as 'turn' — inference questions concentrate on these paragraphs and you can go there first.
Count the questions before you start reading. Ten questions on 700 words justifies a careful 4-minute read; five questions on 700 words does not, and you should skim harder and lean on tags.
traps: Spending 12 or more minutes on one RC set and then rushing 25 other questions. The marks lost elsewhere always exceed the marks gained here.
Treating a Mains long passage like a Prelims one and reading the question stems first — you end up reading the passage twice, which is the one thing you cannot afford.
Guessing the third statement in a three-statement question after verifying two. With 0.25 negative marking, that guess loses more often than it wins; verify all three or leave the question.

Inference options that are true of the world and consistent with the passage but not derivable from it. At Mains these are written more carefully than at Prelims and are correspondingly harder to reject.

Skipping the whole set because the passage looks long. At Mains, RC is 13 of 40 marks, and long passages are usually MORE structured than Prelims ones. Skipping RC caps your English score at roughly 27 out of 40.
Not writing the paragraph tags down because 'I'll remember'. Under a 35-minute clock with 40 questions you will not remember, and the whole technique collapses.
Answering a tone question from the topic rather than the author's language, which is easier to do in a long passage because there is more topic to be distracted by.
e-rc-long.timeTarget: 8 to 10 minutes per 8-10 question long set, i.e. 55-65 seconds per question. Reading a 700-word passage with tags: 4 minutes. Vocabulary sub-question: 25 seconds. Detail with tags: 35-40 seconds. Inference: 60 seconds. Multi-statement: 75-90 seconds.
e-rc-long.masteryCheck: On a 700-word Mains-level passage with 10 questions you finish in under 9.5 minutes with 8 or more correct, having written a tag beside every paragraph and read the passage exactly once. Confirm across three different passages before treating it as reliable.

Central idea / most appropriate title.
3-4 detail questions distributed across paragraphs in passage order.
2-3 inference questions, at least one clustered around a contrast connector.
Tone or author's attitude.
2-3 vocabulary questions on highlighted words, often testing a secondary meaning.
Multi-statement 'which of the following is/are true' with options like 'Only I and III'.
Occasionally: 'which of the following would weaken the author's argument', or a sentence-replacement question on a highlighted portion.
Themes in recent Mains papers have included science and technology, geography and environment, and economics.

No questions, just tagging. 20m untimed: one full 10-question long set with tags, writing the source paragraph beside every answer. 20m timed: one long set with a hard 9-minute stop; whatever is unanswered at 9 minutes stays unanswered, so you feel the cap. 5m: log whether misses were time losses or comprehension losses — at Mains these need opposite fixes.

e-rc-multi.whatItIs: The Mains variant where instead of one long passage you get two or three shorter passages of 200-350 words, each with 3-5 questions. The economics are completely different from a long set, and applying long-passage habits here loses time.
e-rc-multi.coreMethod:
1. UNDERSTAND WHY THE STRATEGY FLIPS. In a short set you pay a fresh comprehension start-up cost for every passage, so the reading-to-question ratio is worse. But each passage is small enough to hold entirely in working memory. Both facts push you toward question-first and away from tagging.
2. QUESTION-FIRST DOES PAY HERE — the opposite of the long-passage rule. For a 300-word passage with 4 questions: read the 4 stems (15 seconds), read the passage once (90-110 seconds), then answer. The stems are cheap to read and tell you exactly what to hold on to.
3. TRIAGE ACROSS SETS BEFORE STARTING. Spend 20 seconds looking at all the short passages and begin with the one whose TOPIC YOU KNOW BEST. There is no requirement to do them in printed order, and topic familiarity is worth 60-90 seconds per set. This is free time and almost nobody takes it.
4. PER-SET BUDGET: 15 seconds on stems + 90-110 seconds reading + 35 seconds per question. A 4-question set is 4 minutes; a 3-question set is 3.2 minutes. Enforce the cap per set, not across the block, or one bad passage silently eats the others.
5. DO NOT SKIM SHORT PASSAGES. Short passages have almost no redundancy — nearly every sentence carries an answer. Read them at a slightly SLOWER pace than a long passage. Skimming only works when there is filler to skip, and here there is none.
6. EXPECT DETAIL TO DOMINATE. Theme and tone questions need length to be fair, so short sets typically run 2-3 detail + 1 vocabulary + at most 1 inference. Attack detail-first here rather than vocabulary-first.
7. COMPARATIVE VARIANTS ('Passage A argues X, Passage B argues Y — identify a point of disagreement'): write the two claims in two columns on the rough sheet BEFORE looking at options, then match. Trying to hold both claims in your head while reading five options is where this variant is lost.
8. DO NOT TAG. Paragraph tagging is a long-passage tool. Using it on a 250-word passage wastes 20 seconds for no retrieval benefit.
tricks: Triage by topic familiarity before you start — this is the highest-return 20 seconds in the whole Mains English paper and costs you nothing.
In a short passage the central idea is almost always in the FIRST or LAST sentence. If a theme question appears, check those two sentences before reading anything else.
If two short sets share a theme (both on climate, both on technology), do them back to back. The vocabulary is already loaded and the second set runs 30-40 seconds faster.

Judge attempt-worthiness by question type, not passage length. A 3-question set that is all detail is worth attempting; a 3-question set with 2 inference plus 1 tone has a reading cost that is not repaid if time is tight.

Read the stems, then read the passage with those stems consciously in mind — in a 250-word passage you will usually recognise the answer sentence as you pass it, and can mark it, answering three questions almost without a second pass.

When two short passages are given as a linked pair (Passage A and Passage B), read BOTH stems before reading either passage. Some questions require both, and discovering that after reading only A costs you a re-read.
traps: Reading all the passages first and then answering all the questions. You will have forgotten passage 1 by the time you finish passage 3, and you will re-read — which destroys the format's only advantage.
Applying long-passage skimming to a short passage. Short Mains passages are dense; skim one and you will miss the single sentence a detail question was built on.
Assuming shorter means easier. Short Mains passages are frequently more abstract and more compressed than long ones — the compression is exactly what makes them hard.
Losing the running clock across three sets because you are only watching the section timer. Set and enforce a per-set cap.
Building a mental map or tags for a 250-word passage. It is wasted effort that feels productive.
Doing the sets in printed order out of habit and hitting the hardest topic first while you still have 30 minutes of paper left.
In comparative A/B variants, answering about passage A when the stem asked about passage B. Circle the letter in the stem before reading options.
e-rc-multi.timeTarget: 4 minutes for a 4-question 300-word set; 3.2 minutes for a 3-question set; 5 minutes for a 5-question 350-word set. Per question inside a short set: 35 seconds. Reading a 300-word passage: 90-110 seconds. Comparative A/B question: 60 seconds.
e-rc-multi.masteryCheck: Given three short passages (250-350 words) with 4 questions each, you complete all twelve questions in under 12.5 minutes with 9 or more correct, having read each passage exactly once and having chosen your own starting order rather than the printed one.

Central idea questions where the answer is the first or last sentence.
Linked-pair variant: Passage A and Passage B on the same theme with questions asking for a point of agreement, disagreement, or which author would support a given statement.
Occasional 'which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument in Passage B'.
Vocabulary on a highlighted word, usually a straightforward synonym at this length.

e-error-1.whatItIs: The foundational format: a sentence split into 3-5 labelled parts, with one part containing a grammatical error and a final option reading 'No error'. About 4-5 questions in Prelims and 5-6 in Mains, and the format that all your grammar study cashes out into.
e-error-1.coreMethod:
1. READ THE SENTENCE ONCE AT NORMAL SPEED WITHOUT HUNTING. Most planted errors sound wrong on a natural read. Hunting rule-by-rule from the first word is slower than reading and then hunting. The scan below is what you do when nothing jumped out.
2. THE 7-POINT SCAN, run in this order because it matches IBPS's actual error frequency:
   (1) VERB AGREEMENT — find the main verb, strip modifiers, check number. Roughly 30% of errors.
   (2) TENSE AND VERB FORM — check time markers; check the participle after each auxiliary (has/have/had + V3, is/are/was/were + V-ing or V3, did/does + V1, modal + V1). ~20%.
   (3) PREPOSITION — check each preposition against its governing verb, adjective or noun. ~15%.
   (4) ARTICLE AND DETERMINER — every singular countable noun needs one; a/an by sound; 'the' with superlatives. ~10%.
   (5) PRONOUN — case after prepositions, agreement with antecedent. ~10%.
   (6) ADJECTIVE/ADVERB — degree errors, -ly after linking verbs, misplaced 'only'. ~8%.
   (7) CONJUNCTION AND PARALLELISM — correlative partners, parallel structure, word order. ~7%.
3. If nothing trips across all seven, choose 'No error'. At Clerk level this is genuinely the correct answer roughly one time in six to eight — it is not a decoy.
4. THE GUESSING RULE (learn this number, it governs the whole section). With five options and 0.25 negative marking: guessing blind is expected value ZERO; eliminating one option gives +0.06; eliminating two gives +0.17; eliminating three gives +0.375. So: NEVER guess with four or five options live; ALWAYS guess once you are down to three or fewer. Convert hesitation into this rule and stop deliberating.
5. Hard cap of 30-35 seconds. If you cannot place the error in that time, apply the guessing rule and move.
tricks: Check the SHORT parts first. Error-detection sentences are split unevenly, and a two-or-three-word part containing a preposition, an article or a comparative is a favourite hiding place that takes three seconds to clear.
If two parts both look wrong, choose the one containing the VERB. IBPS builds the majority of its items around verbs, and agreement/tense errors outnumber everything else roughly two to one.

Memorise these as SHAPES, not rules — you will spot them without parsing: 'discuss about', 'prefer than', 'senior than', 'one of the + singular noun', 'more better', 'informations', 'return back', 'revert back', 'repeat again', 'cope up with', 'comprises of', 'married with', 'since two years', 'each of the boys are', 'the number of ... are', 'hardly ... than', 'lest ... not', 'order for'. Each is a two-second recognition and together they cover a large share of real items.
Never change the MEANING to fix the sentence. If your correction alters what the sentence says, it is not the intended error and you are on the wrong track — restart the scan.
When the error involves agreement across two parts, the answer is the part containing the VERB, not the part containing the subject. Aspirants regularly mark the right error in the wrong part.
Before marking 'No error', do one deliberate check of the prepositions and articles only. These are the errors that survive a natural read, because Indian English normalises them.
traps: Marking a part wrong because it sounds unusual but is grammatically correct — especially inversion after 'Never', 'Seldom', 'Hardly', 'Not only' at the start of a sentence.
Choosing 'No error' as a safety option when you are unsure. If you feel unsure you probably half-saw something; a blind 'No error' is just a one-in-five guess worth exactly zero.

Indian-English usages that read as completely normal: 'revert back to me', 'discuss about the matter', 'cope up with the pressure', 'order for a book', 'good in English' (should be good AT), 'different than' (should be different FROM), 'sit in the table'. These are the errors you will most often read straight past.

Fixating on vocabulary or word choice. Error Detection tests GRAMMAR. If the only thing odd about a part is that a word is unusual, that is almost certainly not the error — word choice is tested separately as word usage and word swap.
Reading only inside part boundaries and never across them. Agreement, correlatives and sequence-of-tense errors span two parts by design.
Spending 60 seconds on one error-detection question. It is worth exactly one mark, the same as a 20-second one, and in a 20-minute sectional paper that is a two-question loss.
Assuming that a long, complex-looking part is more likely to hold the error. Setters frequently hide the fault in the shortest part precisely because candidates skim it.
e-error-1.timeTarget: 30-35 seconds per question in Prelims. A 5-question error-detection set should be finished in under 3 minutes — this block is where you bank early marks.
e-error-1.masteryCheck: You solve 20 single-error sentences in 10 minutes with 17 or more correct, AND for every one you got right you can name the specific rule violated. Naming the rule is the real test — recognising an error you cannot explain does not transfer to new sentences.
questionPatterns: Sentence split into four labelled parts (A)/(B)/(C)/(D) with (E) 'No error' — the standard Prelims format.
Sentence split into three parts with a fourth option 'No error'.
Errors concentrated on subject-verb agreement, tense, prepositions and articles, in that frequency order.
Occasional 'No error' as the genuine key — roughly one item in six to eight.
Sentences deliberately built around a common Indian-English usage that is incorrect in standard grammar.
At Prelims, sentences run 15-25 words; parts are split unevenly with one very short part.

e-error-2.whatItIs: The harder rule set that basic error detection does not cover: parallelism, correlative conjunction pairs, redundancy, misplaced and dangling modifiers, the subjunctive, question tags and word order. These are the items that separate a 15 from a 22 in the English section.
e-error-2.coreMethod:
1. PARALLELISM. Items joined by and/or/but, and everything following a correlative pair, must share grammatical form. 'She likes reading, writing and to paint' -> 'painting'. Structural rule for correlatives: what follows 'not only' and what follows 'but also' must be structurally identical. 'He not only sings but also dances' is right; 'He not only sings but also he dances' is wrong.
2. CORRELATIVE PAIRS — memorise the exact partners; a wrong partner IS the error:
   not only ... but also (never plain 'but')
   either ... or / neither ... nor (never 'or' after neither)
   both ... and (never 'as well as' after both)
   no sooner ... than (never 'when')
   hardly / scarcely / barely ... when or before (never 'than')
   such ... that / so ... that / so ... as (in negatives)
   lest ... should (never with 'not' — 'lest he should fall', not 'lest he should not fall')
   although / though ... yet (never 'but')
   as ... as (affirmative) / so ... as (negative)
   the same ... as / such ... as
   unless and until never take a second negative ('unless you do not come' is wrong)
   since / because / as never pair with 'therefore' or 'so' in the same sentence
3. REDUNDANCY. Learn these as phrases: return back, revert back, repeat again, reverse back, join together, mutual cooperation, free gift, new innovation, past history, final conclusion, close proximity, advance planning, cope up with, discuss about, sufficient enough, more preferable, most unique, ascend up, descend down, two twins, complete monopoly, end result, basic fundamentals, small in size, my personal opinion.
4. MISPLACED AND DANGLING MODIFIERS. An introductory participial phrase must attach to the subject that immediately follows it. 'Walking down the street, the trees looked beautiful' — the trees were not walking. Check the subject right after the comma.
5. SUBJUNCTIVE. After insist, demand, suggest, recommend, propose, order, request, urge, and after 'it is essential/important/necessary/imperative that' — use bare V1: 'He insisted that she GO' (not goes, not went). Also 'wish', 'as if', 'as though', 'it is high time', 'suppose' take V2 or 'were'.
6. QUESTION TAGS (occasional). Opposite polarity, matching auxiliary and subject. 'Let's go, shall we?' 'I am right, aren't I?' Imperative takes 'will you?'
7. WORD ORDER. 'enough' follows the adjective it modifies; adverbs of frequency sit before the main verb but after 'be'; inversion is required after a negative opener ('Never have I seen', 'Seldom does he come', 'Not only did he arrive late...').
tricks: If the sentence contains not only / either / neither / no sooner / hardly / scarcely / lest / although / unless / as...as — go STRAIGHT to the partner word and check it. In sentences containing these, the pair itself is the error roughly 70% of the time. Ten seconds, no full read required.

Scan for lists joined by 'and' and check the SHAPE of the items, not their meaning. If one item is a gerund, one an infinitive and one a plain noun, that is the error. Parallelism is visually detectable once you look at form.
Learn the redundancy list as phrases, not as a rule. 'Return back', 'cope up with', 'sufficient enough' register in two seconds each with no parsing, and at least one usually appears per paper.

After suggest / insist / demand / recommend / propose / essential that, the next verb must be bare V1. Any -s ending or past form there is the error. This is a favourite Mains item and it is entirely mechanical.
'Lest ... should not' — the 'not' is the error, always. Instantly recognisable shape.

If a sentence opens with a comma-separated -ing phrase, look only at the subject after the comma. Mismatch means a dangling modifier, and the error is in the part after the comma, not in the phrase itself.
traps: Marking inversion as wrong. 'Never had I seen such a sight' and 'Seldom does she complain' are both correct, and both look wrong at speed.
'Enter into' is not always redundant — 'enter into an agreement/contract/discussion/negotiation' is correct English. Only 'enter into the room' is wrong.
Over-applying the subjunctive. The bare-V1 rule applies only to 'that'-clauses. 'He suggested going early' is perfectly correct.
'Each and every' is a redundancy in strict grammar but is idiomatic enough that IBPS rarely keys it — do not choose it if a cleaner error exists in the sentence.
Correcting a parallelism issue that is not there because you did not recognise a form — two gerunds where one carries a long modifier still count as parallel.
Reading straight past a redundancy because it sounds natural in Indian English: 'revert back to me', 'discuss about the matter', 'repeat it again'.
Assuming 'not only ... but' without 'also' is always an error. Modern usage permits it; only mark it if the part boundaries make the correlative the clear focus of the item.
e-error-2.timeTarget: 35-40 seconds per question — genuinely slower than basic error detection because the rule set is larger and less visually obvious. Correlative-pair and redundancy items should still resolve in under 15 seconds once the lists are memorised.

e-error-double.whatItIs: A sentence split into 4-5 parts where TWO parts contain errors and the options are combinations ('A and C', 'B and D', 'Only C', 'All parts are correct'). Also appears inverted as 'which of the following parts is/are grammatically correct'. Same one mark, roughly double the time — which makes selection more important than technique here.
e-error-double.coreMethod:
1. DECIDE WHETHER TO ATTEMPT AT ALL. This format pays the same one mark as a 30-second single-error question but costs 50-60 seconds and requires you to be right about two things instead of one. In Prelims it belongs near the end of your attempt order; in Mains it is worth doing but not first.
2. DO NOT HUNT FOR TWO ERRORS. Evaluate each part INDEPENDENTLY and mark it correct / incorrect / unsure. Then read the options and match. Hunting for 'the second error' after finding the first is how you manufacture false positives — you start inventing faults to satisfy the question.
3. WORK PART BY PART IN ORDER, giving each part a maximum of 8 seconds. For each part ask only four things: (i) is there a verb — check agreement and form; (ii) is there a preposition — check the collocation; (iii) is there an article or determiner — check necessity and a/an; (iv) is there a comparative or correlative — check the partner. Nothing else fits in 8 seconds.
4. WRITE YOUR JUDGEMENTS DOWN: A✓ B✗ C? D✓ on the rough sheet. Mental tracking fails under clock pressure and you will re-check a part you already cleared.
5. USE THE OPTIONS AS A CONSTRAINT, NOT A STARTING POINT. Once you are confident about ONE part, eliminate every option that contradicts it. Two confident judgements often uniquely determine the answer even when you are unsure about the remaining parts. This is the real time-saver in this format.
6. FOR THE INVERTED VERSION ('which parts are grammatically CORRECT'), use the identical procedure and invert only at the matching step. Do not translate the question in your head while solving — that is what causes reversal errors.
7. TAKE 'ALL PARTS ARE CORRECT' SERIOUSLY. In double-error sets this option is keyed more often than candidates expect, precisely because they assume the question guarantees two errors.
8. SKIP RULE: at 60 seconds, if you have one confident error and no option isolates it, apply the guessing rule (guess at three or fewer live options, otherwise leave) and move on.
tricks: Anchor on the part you are MOST sure about and eliminate from there. If you are certain part B is wrong, every option not containing B disappears — in a five-option set that typically leaves two, which is a +0.375 expected-value guess and worth taking.
Do the SHORT parts first. They resolve fastest and give you the anchor you need for elimination, which changes the whole economics of the question.

If you find one error and no second candidate after one full pass, re-check the ARTICLES and PREPOSITIONS in every part. Paper-setters routinely pair one structural error with one small-word error, and the small-word one is what survives a first pass.
If two apparent errors sit in adjacent parts and both involve the same verb phrase, it is usually ONE error split across a part boundary. Recount before choosing a two-error option.

Read the instruction line for the exact number of errors. Some variants say 'two parts', some say 'one or more parts'. The second kind allows a single-error answer and candidates lose marks by refusing to select one.
Note your part judgements as symbols on the rough sheet. The five seconds this costs is repaid the moment you look at the options, because you match instead of re-reading.
traps: Manufacturing a second error because the question implies there are two. If the stem guarantees two and you can only find one, the one you found may be the wrong one — re-examine it rather than inventing a partner.
Marking a part wrong for style rather than grammar. Clunky is not incorrect.
Losing track of which parts you have cleared and re-reading them. This is the single largest time leak in this format.
Reading the options first and then trying to confirm a combination. This biases you into seeing errors that are not there, and it is exactly what the option-writers count on.
Spending 90 seconds for one mark. In Prelims that is three single-error questions forgone.
Assuming 'All parts are correct' is a trap option. It is a genuine key often enough to take seriously.
In the inverted 'which parts are correct' version, answering with the incorrect parts because you solved on autopilot. Circle the word 'correct' or 'incorrect' in the instruction before you begin.
e-error-double.timeTarget: 50-60 seconds. Be honest with yourself that this is a 60-second question worth the same one mark as a 30-second one — that arithmetic, not the grammar, is what should drive your decision to attempt it.
e-error-double.masteryCheck: On 10 double-error questions you score 7 or more in under 10 minutes, and on at least 6 of them you reached the answer by eliminating options from ONE confident part judgement rather than by finding both errors independently.
questionPatterns: Sentence in five labelled parts, exactly two containing errors, options given as combinations ('Only A and C', 'Only B and E').
Inverted form: 'Which of the following parts is/are grammatically correct?'

Variant asking 'which part(s) require correction' where the answer may be one, two or three parts.
Typically pairs one structural error (agreement, tense, parallelism) with one small-word error (article, preposition, determiner).
Appears more often in Mains than Prelims, and more often in PO-level papers than Clerk — but does appear at Clerk level.
