e-error-mains.whatItIs: Error detection as it appears in the Mains paper: longer sentences (25-40 words), subtler errors, and rotating instruction formats including 'find the grammatically correct sentence among five'. Mains English is 40 marks that decide merit directly, and there is no interview to recover from.
e-error-mains.coreMethod:
1. READ THE INSTRUCTION LINE AND CIRCLE THE KEY WORD. Mains rotates between at least four instruction types, and each requires the opposite mental operation:
   (a) 'Which part contains an error?'
   (b) 'Which part has NO error?'
   (c) 'Which of the following sentences is grammatically CORRECT?' (five full sentences)
   (d) 'Which of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?'
   Misreading the instruction is the most avoidable loss in Mains English and it happens to good candidates under clock pressure.
2. FOR THE FIVE-FULL-SENTENCES FORMAT — do NOT read them as five sentences. The five options are usually variations of the SAME content differing in only two or three specific spots. Scan across the options to locate the differing spots, then judge only those. This converts five 30-word reads into three 3-word decisions. After RC paragraph tagging, this is the highest-value technique in Mains English.
3. RUN THE STANDARD 7-POINT SCAN (agreement, tense/verb form, preposition, article, pronoun, adjective/adverb, conjunction) and then add the Mains-only layer: subjunctive after suggest/demand/insist/essential that; parallelism across long lists; dangling modifiers; sequence of tenses across three clauses; articles before abstract and uncountable nouns; 'one of the + plural + who + plural verb'; comma splices.
4. IN LONG SENTENCES, FIND THE MAIN CLAUSE FIRST. Identify the main subject and main verb and check them. Then check each subordinate clause separately. Mains sentences hide the error in the main clause while burying it under subordinate detail.
5. UNDERLINE THE MAIN VERB the moment you find it. In a 35-word sentence, losing track of the main verb is how you burn 30 seconds re-reading.
6. BUDGET 45-55 seconds. Mains gives 52.5 seconds per question overall, and error detection deserves roughly that. If the sentence needs a third read, apply the guessing rule and move.
7. APPLY THE ELIMINATION-COUNT RULE STRICTLY at Mains, because these marks decide the merit list: attempt if you can eliminate two or more options; leave it otherwise.
tricks: The compare-the-differing-spots technique for five-full-sentence options. Practise it deliberately on 30 items — it is worth 60 or more seconds per question and most candidates never discover it.
In a 35-word sentence, the error is more often in the FIRST or the LAST clause than in the middle. Setters place it where you read fastest (the opening) or where attention drops (the end).

Any sentence containing a semicolon or a '; however,' construction: check whether both sides are independent clauses. Comma splices and connector misuse are tested at Mains and never at Prelims, so this check is nearly free information.

If the sentence contains a reporting verb (said, told, claimed, argued, stated) plus 'that', check two things only: tense sequence, and whether the reported content is a universal truth that should stay present.
At Mains, 'No error' is a genuine key more often than at Prelims. Do not treat it as a decoy — treating it as one costs real marks in a section that decides your rank.

When two usages in a sentence are both defensible in modern English (different from/than, none is/are, each other/one another, whether/if), that part is almost certainly NOT the intended error. Move past it immediately rather than deliberating.
traps: Misreading 'correct' as 'incorrect' in the instruction. Circle the key word before reading option A — this single habit prevents the most expensive Mains English error.
Applying a Prelims-speed 30-second cap to a 40-word Mains sentence and mis-marking. Mains gives you more time per question; use it here rather than rushing and then having spare time at the end.
Assuming complexity implies error. Long, correct sentences are deliberately used as decoys in the five-sentence format.
Being caught by two acceptable usages and deliberating for 40 seconds over a part that was never the intended answer.
Treating 'No error' as unavailable at Mains because you have been trained on Prelims papers where you rarely selected it.
Reading all five full sentences end to end in the (c)/(d) format instead of comparing differing spots — this is a two-minute question if done wrong and a 40-second question if done right.
Neglecting the subjunctive and dangling-modifier rules because they rarely appear at Prelims. At Mains they appear regularly and are the difference between 5/6 and 3/6 on this block.
e-error-mains.timeTarget: 45-55 seconds per question for the part-based format; 40-50 seconds for the five-full-sentences format once the compare-the-spots technique is automatic (it is 2+ minutes without it).

e-improvement.whatItIs: A phrase in a sentence is underlined or bolded and you choose the best replacement, with 'No improvement required' as a live option. Also called phrase replacement. It tests the same grammar as error detection but requires you to produce the correction, not just locate the fault.
e-improvement.coreMethod:
1. READ THE WHOLE SENTENCE, not just the underlined part. The fault is frequently a mismatch between the underlined portion and something OUTSIDE it — the subject (for agreement), a time marker (for tense), or a correlative partner.
2. PREDICT THE CORRECTION BEFORE LOOKING AT THE OPTIONS. Say the fixed version in your head, then find the option closest to it. This is the core discipline of the question type. Reading the options first makes all five sound plausible and roughly doubles your time.
3. DIAGNOSE THE CATEGORY, in IBPS frequency order: verb form or tense -> preposition -> correlative or conjunction -> parallelism -> redundancy -> pronoun case -> article -> word order -> idiom. Naming the category tells you what to look for in the options.
4. ELIMINATE MEANING-CHANGERS. Options that alter what the sentence says are wrong even when they are grammatically perfect. Improvement questions test grammar and idiom, not rewriting. Cross out anything that adds or removes information.
5. PREFER THE SHORTEST GRAMMATICALLY CORRECT OPTION. Bank answer keys favour concision. Options padded with 'in order to', 'due to the fact that', 'the reason being that', 'on account of the fact' are decoys nearly every time.
6. SUBSTITUTE AND RE-READ. Put your chosen option back into the full sentence and read it once. Five seconds, and it catches the 'right fix, wrong tense' trap that is otherwise invisible.
7. 'NO IMPROVEMENT REQUIRED' is correct roughly one time in six. Choose it only after running the diagnosis — but do choose it when the diagnosis comes back clean.
tricks: Predict-then-match is the whole game. It is the difference between a 30-second solve and a 70-second one, and it is a habit rather than a piece of knowledge — you have to force it for two weeks before it sticks.

Scan the underlined portion for the usual suspects in five seconds: is there a preposition, a verb form, a correlative word, a comparative, or a pronoun? Whichever one is present is what the question is testing. You now know the category before reading a single option.

If the underlined part contains 'being', be immediately suspicious. 'Being' is wrong in the large majority of bank improvement items — 'The work being done by him' -> 'The work done by him'. A one-word signal with a high hit rate.

If the five options differ only in their preposition, you are being tested on a collocation, not on logic. Go straight to the governing verb or adjective and recall the pair; do not reason about meaning.

If there is a time marker OUTSIDE the underlined portion (since, ago, by the time, last year, already), the answer is a tense fix. You can often select it from the options without fully parsing the sentence.

When two options are structurally identical and differ only in formality of a word, choose the more standard and idiomatic one. Bank keys avoid rare vocabulary in improvement questions — the answer is almost never the fanciest option.
traps: Choosing the option that 'sounds better' stylistically instead of the one that fixes the actual grammatical fault. Style is not tested; grammar and idiom are.
Ignoring everything outside the underlined portion — especially the subject, which determines agreement, and time markers, which determine tense.

Picking an option that fixes the identified error but introduces a new one. This is exactly what the substitute-and-re-read step exists to catch, and skipping that step is the most common single cause of loss here.
Being afraid of 'No improvement required'. At Clerk level a meaningful fraction of these genuinely need no change, and candidates who never select it are systematically losing those marks.
Options that are perfectly correct English but change the meaning — swapping 'should' for 'must', 'many' for 'all', 'may' for 'will'. Grammatical correctness is necessary, not sufficient.
Assuming the underlined part must be wrong because it was underlined. The format explicitly allows it to be right.
Reading all five options before forming your own correction, which is the single habit that makes this question type slow.
e-improvement.timeTarget: 25-35 seconds per question. A 5-question improvement set should be done in under 3 minutes. Anything over 45 seconds means you skipped the prediction step and are comparing options against each other instead of against a target.
e-improvement.masteryCheck: You solve 20 improvement questions in 10 minutes with 17 or more correct, AND in at least 15 of the 20 you had predicted the correction in your head before reading the options. Track the prediction count explicitly — accuracy without prediction will not survive exam pressure.
questionPatterns: A phrase underlined or bolded within a sentence, five replacement options, with 'No improvement/No correction required' as one option.
Verb-form and tense fixes where the time marker sits outside the underlined portion.
Preposition collocation fixes where all five options differ only by the preposition.
Correlative pair fixes: the underlined part contains one half of a not only/either/no sooner pair.
Redundancy removal: the underlined part contains 'return back', 'cope up with', 'sufficient enough'.
'Being' constructions that need to be simplified.
Parallelism fixes in a list.

e-vocab.whatItIs: Every question type where the answer depends on what a word means in a specific sentence: RC synonyms and antonyms, word usage, word swap, single and double fillers, and misspelt words. Note the framing — IBPS tests words in context, so word-list memorisation transfers poorly and context substitution transfers completely.
e-vocab.coreMethod:
1. STOP LEARNING ISOLATED WORD LISTS. The same word is right in one sentence and wrong in another; the exam tests fit, not recall. The method below is substitution, not memory.
2. RC SYNONYM/ANTONYM: go to the word, read its sentence plus the one before. Determine POLARITY first — is the required word positive, negative or neutral, based on the surrounding language? Eliminate every option with the wrong polarity; this typically kills two or three options in five seconds. Then substitute the survivors into the actual sentence and pick the one that reads naturally.
3. WORD USAGE ('in which sentence(s) is the word used correctly'): check the PART OF SPEECH first. Most wrong sentences misuse the word as the wrong part of speech — a noun used as a verb, an adjective used as an adverb. This resolves about half of these questions without knowing the precise meaning.
4. WORD SWAP (two words must be interchanged): locate the two content words that feel semantically misplaced, then test only SAME-PART-OF-SPEECH pairs — noun with noun, verb with verb, adjective with adjective. Swap them mentally and re-read. If the sentence now expresses a coherent idea, that is the answer. Never test all possible pairs; that is what makes candidates slow here.
5. FILLERS AND DOUBLE FILLERS: fill the blank you are SURE about first and eliminate on that basis alone. Never try to satisfy both blanks simultaneously. Then check connector logic — but/however/although/yet demands a contrast between the two halves; and/moreover/furthermore demands continuation; because/since/as demands cause.
6. MISSPELT WORDS: the exam draws from a small pool. Learn the trouble patterns rather than individual words — double letters (accommodate, occurrence, necessary, embarrass, recommend, occasion, committee, harass, tomorrow, address, aggressive), -ceed/-cede/-sede (only proceed, succeed, exceed take -ceed; supersede is the only -sede), -ance vs -ence (existence, persistence, maintenance, perseverance, independence), and silent-letter words (privilege, definitely, separate, government, environment, February, restaurant, entrepreneur, liaison, questionnaire, rhythm, bureaucracy, conscience).
7. BUILD VOCABULARY FROM WHAT YOU READ. Every unknown word from your daily editorial goes into a notebook WITH THE SENTENCE it appeared in, not with a dictionary definition alone. Twenty words a week from real reading beats a hundred from a list, because contextual fit is the thing being tested.
tricks: Polarity-first elimination is the fastest move in the whole vocabulary area. Decide positive/negative/neutral before you consider precise meaning — it removes two or three options in five seconds with no vocabulary knowledge at all.

Decode unknown words by affix: mal-, mis-, dis-, un-, in-, non-, anti- signal negative; bene-, pro-, eu- signal positive; -ous and -ful signal adjective; -tion, -ment, -ness, -ity signal noun; -ise, -ify, -en signal verb. Enough to place an unknown word's polarity and part of speech in three seconds, which is often enough to answer.

In double fillers, count the options first. If three options share the same FIRST word, the second blank is the discriminator — solve the second blank only, and ignore the first entirely. And vice versa. A pure structural shortcut that saves 20 or more seconds per question.

In word-swap questions, the swapped pair is almost always in DIFFERENT clauses of the sentence, not adjacent to each other. Look across the comma or conjunction first rather than scanning left to right.
If a synonym question's options include two words that are near-synonyms of EACH OTHER, neither is usually the key — the answer key avoids ambiguity. Look at the other three first.

Learn the ~30 confusable pairs that recur in bank papers: affect/effect, principal/principle, complement/compliment, stationary/stationery, adapt/adopt, elicit/illicit, eminent/imminent, moral/morale, council/counsel, cite/site/sight, precede/proceed, accept/except, assure/ensure/insure, discreet/discrete, loose/lose, farther/further, lie/lay, historic/historical, economic/economical, continual/continuous, credible/credulous, ingenious/ingenuous, judicial/judicious, negligent/negligible, official/officious, respectable/respectful/respective, sensible/sensitive. These are pure marks and they repeat across years.
traps: Choosing the dictionary-primary meaning instead of the contextual one. RC synonym questions frequently use a secondary sense of a common word, and the primary meaning is always offered as an option.
Translating the word to Hindi and back to choose an option. The register shifts in translation and you end up picking a word of the wrong formality.

Selecting a word that fits grammatically but carries the wrong connotation: frugal versus stingy, confident versus arrogant, assertive versus aggressive, inexpensive versus cheap. Connotation is what these questions are built on.

In word swap, choosing a pair that makes the sentence grammatical but changes the intended meaning. The correct swap RESTORES the sentence's original logical sense — if your swap produces a sentence that is fine but says something odd, it is wrong.
Memorising lists you never encounter in context. You will recognise the word in the option and still not know whether it fits the sentence, which is exactly what is being tested.
In fillers, committing on the strength of the first word without checking the second. Always verify both before selecting, even when the first word is a perfect fit.
Assuming misspelt-word questions need broad spelling knowledge. They draw from a narrow, repeating pool — learn the pool rather than trying to become a good speller.

e-cloze.whatItIs: A 6-10 line editorial paragraph with 5-6 numbered blanks; you pick one word per blank from five options. It tests collocation and paragraph direction far more than it tests vocabulary size.
e-cloze.coreMethod:
1. READ THE WHOLE PASSAGE ONCE AT SPEED (25-30 sec) without stopping at any blank. You are hunting two things only: the topic in one word, and the tone (positive / negative / neutral / mixed). Do not attempt any blank on this pass.
2. Find the SPINE sentence — the one that states the passage's main claim. Every theme-carrying blank must agree in tone with it.
3. Solve in EASY-FIRST order, not left to right. Three tiers: (a) grammar-forced blanks (a blank followed by a fixed preposition, a blank right after a comma or at sentence-start = connector, a blank after an article), (b) collocation blanks (blank sits next to a noun/verb that only pairs with certain words), (c) pure-meaning blanks. Do tier (a) fully, then (b), then (c).
4. For EACH blank, before you read the options, name the part of speech the slot requires. Look only at the word immediately before and immediately after. 'the ___ of' = noun. 'has ___' = past participle. 'to ___' = base verb. 'very ___' = adjective or adverb. 'been ___ by' = past participle.
5. Kill options on part of speech. At Clerk level this usually removes two of five instantly and costs you three seconds.
6. Apply the DIRECTION test: find the nearest connector to the blank (but, however, yet, although, despite, moreover, therefore, hence, because, since). If it is a contrast connector, the blank's polarity must be opposite to the neighbouring clause. If continuation, same polarity.
7. Plug the survivor in and read the ENTIRE sentence, not the clause. Wrong answers in IBPS cloze are built to work locally and break at the far end of the sentence.
8. If two survive, take the plainer, more common word and move. Hard cap: 15 seconds on any single blank. Never let one blank eat the set.
tricks: If blank 1 sits in the first sentence, skip it outright and do blanks 2-6 first. By the time you return, the passage's meaning is fully loaded and blank 1 solves in five seconds. Blank 1 is structurally the hardest because it has the least prior context — solving it first is the single biggest time leak in this topic.

Any blank immediately after a comma, semicolon, or at the start of a sentence is a connector blank ~80% of the time. Scan the five options for however / moreover / therefore / thus / hence / although / consequently and answer it without reading much context. 5 seconds, 1 mark.

If two of the five options are synonyms of each other, BOTH are wrong. IBPS cannot ship a question with two defensible answers. Cross them both out and choose from the remaining three — this converts a 1-in-5 into a 1-in-3 in two seconds.

Preposition-locked verbs are free marks. If the word after the blank is a fixed preposition, only one option legally takes it: result IN, consist OF, comply WITH, capable OF, prone TO, attribute TO, adhere TO, contribute TO, refrain FROM, deprive OF, accuse OF, insist ON, rely ON.
Article agreement: if the blank is preceded by 'an', the answer starts with a vowel SOUND; if preceded by 'a', it does not. Free elimination requiring zero comprehension.

Countability filter: 'a ___ of problems' needs a countable collective (number / range / host / spate), 'much ___' needs an uncountable noun. Check the quantifier before the blank and half the options die.

Pre-load the recurring theme vocabulary. IBPS Clerk cloze runs on a small pool: growth, decline, reform, policy, impact, sustainable, mitigate, curb, bolster, hamper, address, ensure, undermine, significant, adverse, robust. Recognition beats reasoning.
traps: Solving strictly left to right. This is the most expensive habit in the topic and the one that makes aspirants run out of time on blank 5 and 6, which are usually the easiest.
Choosing the biggest-sounding word. Clerk-level cloze answers are ordinary. If 'increase' and 'burgeon' both fit, it is 'increase'.
Reading only up to the blank and ignoring the clause AFTER it. The distractor is constructed to fit the left half perfectly and contradict the right half.
Missing a negation ('not', 'hardly', 'fail to', 'no longer') inside the blank's own sentence. The negation flips the polarity the blank needs, and aspirants routinely pick the un-flipped word.

Treating blanks as independent when the paragraph has a contrast pivot. If blank 3 is 'however', blank 4's tone must be opposite to blank 2's. Blanks in a cloze are a chain, not five separate questions.
Picking a word because you learnt it last week. Familiarity is not evidence of fit.
Burning 40 seconds on one unknown blank and then rushing the remaining three. A cloze is a set — one lost blank is 1 mark, a rushed set is 3.
e-cloze.timeTarget: 5-6 blanks in 100-130 seconds TOTAL including the 25-30 sec first read. That is ~20-22 sec per mark. Budget cloze as a SET, never per question. If you are past 150 sec, mark what you have and leave.

e-cloze-replace.whatItIs: A passage where each blank is immediately followed by a word in bold. You choose the option that should replace the bold word, or option (E) 'No replacement required' if the bold word is already correct. It tests whether you can leave a correct word alone.
e-cloze-replace.coreMethod:
1. Read the passage ONCE treating every bold word as if it were correct (20-25 sec). You want topic and tone only. Do not evaluate as you read.
2. For each bold word run TEST 1 — LEGALITY: is this word grammatically permissible in this slot? Check part of speech (via its suffix), tense against the paragraph's tense, singular/plural against its subject, and the preposition that follows it. If it fails legality, a replacement is definitely needed and you now only read options of the correct grammatical form — usually two of four.
3. If it survives TEST 1, run TEST 2 — COLLOCATION: does this exact word normally sit next to its neighbour in newspaper English? 'heavy rain' yes, 'strong rain' no. 'make a decision' yes, 'do a decision' no. 'pose a threat' yes, 'put a threat' no. Collocation failure means replacement needed even though grammar is fine.
4. If it survives TEST 2, run TEST 3 — POLARITY: does the word's positive/negative charge match the sentence and the paragraph's direction? A negative-charged bold word inside a sentence praising something needs replacement.
5. Passes all three tests: mark (E). Do not manufacture an error.
6. When replacing, substitute the candidate and read the whole clause. The correct replacement makes the sentence read MORE NATURALLY, not more impressively.
7. Attack order: broken-grammar bold words first (fast and certain), then collocation failures, then polarity. Leave the ones where you are hesitating between the bold word and one option for last.
tricks: Count your (E)s. In a 5-blank replacement set, 'No replacement required' is correct roughly once or twice. If you have marked zero (E)s, go back and re-run TEST 1 on your two shakiest blanks — you are reflex-changing. If you have marked three or more, you are under-reading and missing planted errors.

Suffix-to-slot matching solves blanks without any vocabulary knowledge. -tion / -ment / -ness / -ity / -ance = noun slot. -ive / -ous / -ful / -al / -ic = adjective slot. -ly = adverb slot. -ate / -ise / -ify = verb slot. A suffix that mismatches the slot is an instant 'replacement needed' and instantly filters options to the right shape.

Tense sweep: read only the verbs of the paragraph in sequence, ignoring everything else. If the paragraph runs in past tense and one bold verb is present, that blank is solved in three seconds and the answer is simply the past form sitting in the options.

If two of the four options are the same root word in different forms (reduce / reduction, sustain / sustainable), the question is testing part of speech, not meaning. Decide the slot's part of speech and answer without knowing what any word means.

If the bold word is half of a fixed multi-word phrase ('in the WAKE of', 'on the BRINK of', 'at the EXPENSE of', 'in the FACE of'), it will look wrong in isolation and be right in place. Always read three words either side of a bold word before judging it.
traps: Assuming every bold word must be replaced. This is the entire design of the format — option (E) exists to punish reflex-changing, and it is where most marks are lost.
Replacing a word because you personally would have phrased it differently. The test is 'is it wrong', not 'is it my preference'.
Judging the bold word in isolation instead of inside its phrase. Half the correct bold words look odd alone.
Going to meaning before grammar. The legality check takes three seconds and resolves most blanks; meaning analysis takes twenty and often resolves nothing.
Choosing a replacement that would force the article before it to change (a → an). If the surrounding text is fixed and your option breaks the article, it is the wrong option.

Applying prelims pace here. Replacement cloze needs 20-30% more time per blank than blank-type cloze because you are evaluating five candidates, not four — budget for it instead of rushing and misfiring.

e-cloze-mains.whatItIs: A longer, denser editorial passage where the five options for each blank are near-synonyms, so grammar rarely separates them. The discriminator becomes collocation and register, not meaning. It is also the exact skill that powers the Mains 'Word Replacement' questions.
e-cloze-mains.coreMethod:
1. Accept the shift: in Prelims cloze, grammar decides. In Mains cloze, grammar has already been neutralised by the setter — all five options usually fit the slot grammatically. Do not waste a pass looking for part-of-speech mismatches; they have been removed.
2. Read the passage once (35-40 sec) mapping the ARGUMENT SHAPE, not the facts: where does the author state the problem, where is the pivot, where is the verdict. Physically note the connectors (yet, notwithstanding, consequently, in contrast, that said).
3. For each blank, name the exact word it must attach to — its governing noun or verb. Then ask one question: which of these five have I actually SEEN standing next to that word in newspaper English?
4. Use the REGISTER filter. Mains passages are editorial and the answer pool is small and predictable: mitigate, exacerbate, underscore, bolster, curb, spur, hinge on, grapple with, usher in, erode, hamper, stem, entail, warrant, undermine, compound. If one option is from this pool and the others are ordinary conversational words, the editorial word is usually right — this is the opposite of the Prelims heuristic and you must switch it deliberately.
5. Use INTENSITY matching. When all five options mean roughly the same thing, look for a nearby intensity marker. 'Marginal', 'modest', 'slight' nearby demands a mild verb; 'sharp', 'drastic', 'unprecedented' demands a strong one.
6. Preposition after the blank is still the single fastest filter, and it survives into Mains: '___ to the crisis' admits responded / contributed / led; '___ for the crisis' admits blamed / accounted. Check it before anything semantic.
7. Two-blanks-in-one-sentence variants: solve the blank with fewer legal candidates first and let it constrain the other. Never try to satisfy both simultaneously.
8. TRIAGE RULE: with 35 minutes for 40 Mains questions and RC consuming 16-18 of them, a cloze set must complete in under 2 minutes or be abandoned. Decide at blank 2 — if you have made no confident call by then, leave the set and take the marks elsewhere.
tricks: Memorise 15 editorial verb+noun collocations and you cover a disproportionate share of both Mains cloze and Mains word-replacement answers: curb inflation, bolster growth, exacerbate the crisis, underscore the need, mitigate the impact, spur demand, address concerns, pose a threat, reap benefits, bridge the gap, stem the tide, usher in reform, erode confidence, hamper progress, trigger a decline. This is the highest return-per-minute memorisation in the entire English section.

Scan the options for negative prefixes before reading them for meaning. A single un- / dis- / mis- / non- that you skim past reverses the answer, and Mains setters plant exactly this because tired eyes drop prefixes.

When two options survive and you cannot separate them, check which one the passage's OWN vocabulary is closer to. Editorial writers stay in one register within a paragraph; the answer usually matches the words already on the page.

If a blank is inside a subordinate clause introduced by 'while' or 'even as', the blank's polarity must oppose the main clause. This one structure appears in most Mains passages and is worth a free mark.
Do Mains cloze AFTER reading comprehension, never before. RC is 16-18 marks and cloze is 5. If you run short, you want the shortfall to land on the 5, not the 17.
traps: Trying to fully comprehend the passage. Mains passages are deliberately dense; you need the local sentence and the direction of the argument, nothing more. Comprehension-chasing is how a 2-minute set becomes a 5-minute set.
Choosing the hardest word because the paper is Mains. The paper's difficulty is not the answer's difficulty — the setter raises difficulty by making the DISTRACTORS harder, not the key.

Carrying the Prelims heuristic 'pick the plainer word' into Mains unchanged. In Mains the plainer word is often the trap, because the passage's register is formal. You must consciously flip this rule between the two exams.
Letting one unknown-vocabulary blank destroy the set. Guess it on tone alone and move — the other four blanks are still fully winnable and are worth 4 marks.
Ignoring 'that said', 'to be sure', 'granted' — these are contrast pivots that look like filler and flip the polarity of everything after them.
Attempting a Mains cloze set at all when you are behind pace. It is the most abandonable set in the Mains English paper.

e-phrase.whatItIs: A sentence with one bolded or underlined phrase and four alternatives plus 'No correction required'. It is error spotting with the error location already given to you, which makes it the fastest-scoring grammar format in the paper.
e-phrase.coreMethod:
1. Read the ENTIRE sentence, not just the underlined part. IBPS routinely puts the trigger outside the underline — the real subject sits ten words earlier, or a tense marker appears at the end.
2. Run the error checklist in THIS fixed order, ordered by how often IBPS actually uses each at Clerk level:
   (a) SUBJECT-VERB AGREEMENT. Find the real subject by mentally deleting every prepositional phrase. 'The list of items IS' not 'are'. 'One of the boys HAS' not 'have'. 'Each / every / neither / either' take singular.
   (b) TENSE SEQUENCE. For two past actions, the earlier takes had + V3. 'Since' or 'for' with a duration forces present perfect or present perfect continuous. Reported speech shifts tense back one step.
   (c) PREPOSITION. Fixed verb+preposition and adjective+preposition pairs.
   (d) PARALLELISM. Every item in a list must share form: 'reading, writing and speaking', never 'reading, writing and to speak'.
   (e) ARTICLE. a / an by sound not spelling; 'the' with superlatives and unique things; zero article with abstract and uncountable nouns used generally.
   (f) PRONOUN. Number and antecedent agreement; 'everyone... his or her' not 'their' in exam English.
   (g) MODIFIER PLACEMENT. A participial opener must attach to the subject that follows: 'Walking down the road, THE TREE fell' is wrong.
   (h) CORRELATIVE PAIRS. not only...but also; no sooner...than; hardly/scarcely...when; lest...should; too...to; such...that; so...that.
   (i) REDUNDANCY. return back, repeat again, more better, reason is because, discuss about, cope up with, comprises of.
3. NAME THE ERROR TYPE OUT LOUD IN YOUR HEAD before you look at the options. This is the whole technique. Once you have said 'subject-verb', you read the options only for the verb and discard three at a glance.
4. Read the options VERTICALLY. Compare only the words that DIFFER between options and ignore everything identical. This alone saves 8-10 seconds a question.
5. Substitute the survivor into the full sentence and read once end to end.
6. If the full checklist finds nothing, mark 'No correction required'. Do not invent an error to feel productive.
tricks: Options in this format almost always split into two camps — two options say 'has been', two say 'have been'. Decide the CAMP first with one grammar rule, then decide within the camp on a second, smaller difference. Two binary decisions are far faster than five comparisons.
If the underlined phrase contains a preposition, check the preposition first. It is the single most frequently tested feature at Clerk level and resolves the question before you read anything else.
'Being' inside an option is wrong far more often than right at Clerk level. Deprioritise those options and read them last.

Memorise the ~25 Indian-English error phrases IBPS recycles year after year: discuss about, cope up with, comprises of, return back, revert back, order for, request for (as verb), married with, comprised of, one of the + singular noun, the reason is because, more superior, different than, avail of (correct) vs avail (incorrect alone), in spite of + clause, despite of, according to me, myself so-and-so. Recognising one of these ends the question instantly.

An option that changes the MEANING rather than the grammar is a distractor. The correct replacement preserves the sentence's intent exactly — if an option makes the sentence say something different, discard it without grammatical analysis.
When two options are both grammatical, the shorter one wins more often than not. Use only as a tiebreaker, never as a primary rule.
traps: Choosing an option that is grammatically clean but alters the intended meaning. This is the most common way strong grammar students lose this question.

Missing that the subject is separated from the verb by a long modifying phrase. 'The quality of the products manufactured in these factories HAS declined' — the plural 'products' and 'factories' are bait.
Marking 'No correction required' out of fatigue, or never marking it out of fear. At Clerk level it is correct roughly one time in five or six. Both extremes cost marks.
Fixing the flagged error while the option quietly introduces a second one. Read the full option, never the changed fragment alone.

Rejecting an option because it sounds unnatural to an Indian ear. Spoken Indian English differs from exam English at exactly the tested points — 'discuss about' and 'cope up with' sound right and are wrong.
Not noticing that the underline includes a conjunction or punctuation mark, which changes the clause structure of the whole sentence.
Treating 'Sentence Improvement' as a different topic. It is the identical format under another label and appeared as such in IBPS Clerk Prelims 2025.
e-phrase.timeTarget: 20-25 seconds per question. A 3-4 question block should close in 75-100 seconds. If a question passes 35 seconds, mark your best camp-level guess and move.

e-phrase-swap.whatItIs: A sentence containing three or four bold PHRASES that have been shuffled out of position. You choose which two phrases must be interchanged to make the sentence coherent. It is a grammatical slot-matching puzzle, not a comprehension task.
e-phrase-swap.coreMethod:
1. Read the sentence once at normal pace. Do not try to repair it yet — only register WHERE the sentence stops making sense. That location is your entry point.
2. Extract the skeleton: subject + main verb + object. If a bold phrase is occupying the subject slot but is obviously object-type material (or vice versa), you have one end of the swap.
3. MATCH BY GRAMMATICAL SLOT, which is the core of the method. A prepositional phrase can only swap with another prepositional phrase. A noun phrase with a noun phrase. A verb phrase with a verb phrase. Any option pairing two phrases of different grammatical type is almost certainly wrong, and this single rule kills most of the option list before you think about meaning.
4. Then match by SEMANTIC FIT. Read the sentence with just that one pair interchanged. If it reads clean from start to finish, mark it. You should need at most two trial substitutions.
5. When testing a pair, read ONLY the two affected clauses, not the whole sentence. Re-reading a 30-word sentence four times is where the time goes.
6. If two pairs both appear to work, choose the one that fixes the EARLIEST point of incoherence. IBPS builds these so that exactly one interchange repairs the entire sentence.
tricks: Work backwards from the OPTION LIST, not from the sentence. There are only four or five candidate pairs on offer; testing pairs is far faster than diagnosing the sentence unaided. Test first the pair whose two phrases are most similar in grammatical shape.

The two phrases that must move are almost always WRONG for where they sit but IDENTICAL in grammatical role to each other. If two bold phrases both open with the same preposition ('in the...', 'in the...'), or both are '-ing' phrases, they are prime candidates — spot them by shape before reading a word of meaning.

Look for the phrase producing obvious nonsense — an abstract noun performing a physical action, a time expression in a place slot. That phrase is one half of the pair; find its partner purely by slot type.

You do not need to know what the sentence is about. Slot-matching is topic-blind, which means an unfamiliar subject (macroeconomics, marine biology) costs you nothing. Do not let unfamiliar vocabulary make you skip this question.

Check the words immediately BORDERING each bold phrase. Those border words determine what grammatical type belongs there, and reading four pairs of border words is faster than reading the sentence twice.
traps: Trying to repair the sentence in your head before looking at the options. The options constrain you to four specific pairs — use that constraint, it is a gift.
Choosing a swap that fixes the first half and quietly breaks the second. Always read PAST the swap point to the end of the sentence.
Assuming three phrases are out of place. In this format exactly TWO move, unless an option explicitly states otherwise.
Being scared off by unknown vocabulary. The method never requires you to know a single word's meaning.
Ignoring a 'no interchange required' option where one is offered — occasionally the sentence is already correct and the reflex to swap something costs a quarter mark.
Confusing this with word swap and looking at single words. Here the unit is a multi-word phrase, and single-word comparisons will produce nonsense.
e-phrase-swap.timeTarget: 25-35 seconds per question. Slower than single-word swap because each phrase is longer to re-read — budget honestly rather than assuming word-swap pace.

e-fillers.whatItIs: A standalone sentence with one or two blanks and five options. Single fillers give one word per option; double fillers give a word pair, and both halves must be right. It is the fastest-scoring format in the entire English section.
e-fillers.coreMethod:
1. Read the sentence TO THE END before looking at any option. In IBPS fillers the disambiguating clue is usually AFTER the blank, not before it.
2. Find the SIGNAL. Every filler sentence has one: a connector (but, yet, although, despite, while, however = contrast; and, moreover, also, besides, since, because = continuation), or punctuation (a colon or dash means the blank is defined by what follows; a semicolon means the two halves balance).
3. PREDICT YOUR OWN WORD before reading the options. Say it silently. Then look for the option nearest your prediction. This is the single largest speed gain in the topic — it converts a five-way comparison into a one-way match.
4. Determine the part of speech the slot needs from the words either side, and kill mismatched options.
5. Check POLARITY. Count the negations in the clause (not, never, hardly, fail to, far from, no longer). Each one flips the charge the blank needs.
6. FOR DOUBLE BLANKS — solve the EASIER blank first, which is almost always the second one because it has more context around it. Eliminate every option that fails on that blank. Only then check the survivors on the harder blank. Never attempt to satisfy both simultaneously.
7. Remember the double-blank rule that decides most of them: both words come from the SAME option. One clearly wrong half kills the entire option even if the other half is perfect. So you are looking for a reason to REJECT, not a reason to accept.
8. Substitute and read the whole sentence once. Mark and move.
tricks: In double fillers, scan the SECOND element of all five options first, as a vertical column, before reading the sentence twice. Typically three of five die on the second blank alone, leaving a two-way check. Working blank 1 first is slower because blank 1 sits early in the sentence with less context.

Contrast signals are the highest-yield clue in the topic. 'Although / despite / in spite of / while / notwithstanding / on the contrary' means the blank must OPPOSE the other clause's charge. Spotting one of these decides most single fillers before you evaluate any word's meaning.

Preposition-locked blanks are instant marks: the preposition immediately after the blank forces the answer. Learn the top verb+preposition and adjective+preposition pairs — susceptible TO, indicative OF, conducive TO, averse TO, contingent ON, tantamount TO, devoid OF, fraught WITH, replete WITH, bereft OF.
If two options are near-synonyms, both are wrong. IBPS cannot ship two defensible answers. Cross out the pair — a two-second move that turns 1-in-5 into 1-in-3.
If the blank is preceded by 'an', the answer starts with a vowel sound. If preceded by 'a', it does not. Requires zero comprehension.
Comparatives need a basis. If an option is 'more X' but the sentence contains no 'than' and no comparison, discard it.

Learn the 25 filler words banks recycle and half the questions become recognition rather than reasoning: crucial, significant, adverse, sustainable, resilient, robust, imminent, prevalent, ambiguous, feasible, viable, stringent, lucrative, inevitable, prudent, detrimental, sceptical, unprecedented, plausible, mitigate, curb, bolster, hamper, spur, deter.
traps: Reading only up to the blank. In most IBPS fillers the clue is downstream, and stopping at the blank is the single commonest cause of a wrong answer here.
Choosing a word that fits the immediate phrase but contradicts the sentence's polarity — picking 'improved' in a sentence whose second half reports widespread losses.
In double fillers, locking onto blank 1 and then forcing blank 2 to fit around your choice. Let the easier blank do the eliminating.
Selecting on sophistication. Clerk-level filler answers are ordinary words; the exotic option is usually the distractor.
Missing the article before the blank and its sound agreement.
Assuming a plural noun after the blank needs a special adjective form. English adjectives do not inflect for number — if you are looking there, you are looking in the wrong place.
Treating double fillers as twice the work of single fillers. Done correctly with the reject-first method they take about 50% longer, not 100%.
e-fillers.timeTarget: 15-20 seconds per single filler; 25-30 seconds per double filler. A 4-5 question block should close in 80-100 seconds. This is your fastest format — it is where you buy time for the sets.
e-fillers.masteryCheck: You complete 10 single fillers in 3 minutes with 9 correct, AND 10 double fillers in 4 minutes with 8 correct — and on the double fillers you can state which blank you used to do the eliminating on each question.

e-parajumble.whatItIs: Five sentences given out of order that must be arranged into a coherent paragraph, usually with five questions asking which sentence occupies which position. It is a linkage puzzle solved on pronouns, articles and connectors, not on comprehension.
e-parajumble.coreMethod:
1. Read all five sentences once, fast (~30 sec). Name the topic in one word. Do not attempt to sequence yet.
2. FIND THE OPENER BY DISQUALIFICATION, which is faster than finding it directly. A sentence CANNOT be the opener if it contains: a pronoun with no antecedent inside itself (he, she, it, they, this, these, those, such, the former); a continuation connector (however, moreover, therefore, thus, also, besides, consequently, on the other hand, in addition, as a result); a definite article introducing a noun not yet named ('the scheme' when no scheme has been mentioned); or a backward-looking comparative ('a better one', 'the latter'). Strike these out ruthlessly. Usually only one or two candidates survive.
3. The genuine opener typically carries a general statement, or introduces a full noun with its identifying apposition ('The Reserve Bank of India, the country's central bank, ...'), or sets a time or scene.
4. BUILD MANDATORY PAIRS rather than sequencing everything. Look for: noun → pronoun (one sentence names 'the committee', another says 'it recommended'); indefinite article → definite article ('a new policy' must precede 'the policy'); cause → effect (therefore / as a result / consequently); question → answer; general claim → 'for instance' example; 'firstly' → 'secondly'.
5. NOW GO TO THE OPTIONS. This is the crucial move: you do not need the complete order. Take your ONE most confident pair and eliminate every option that does not contain it, adjacent and in that direction. Two or three options typically die on a single pair.
6. If two options survive, find a second pair, or identify the closer — conclusions carry 'thus / hence / therefore / in conclusion', or make an evaluative or forward-looking statement.
7. Read your chosen order once end to end to confirm the flow, then answer all five positional questions from it.
tricks: ALWAYS look at the answer options before you sequence anything. If every option begins with the same sentence, the opener has been handed to you free — skip the disqualification step entirely and go straight to pairing. This happens often and saves 20-30 seconds.

Pronoun-antecedent is the most reliable pair-maker in IBPS para jumbles. Find any sentence opening with It / They / This / These / He / She / Such, then find the sentence containing the noun it must refer to. That noun sentence sits immediately before it in the great majority of cases.
Article progression is nearly as reliable and takes five seconds: scan only for 'a/an' + noun and 'the' + the same noun. The indefinite sentence must precede the definite one.
Chronology short-circuits everything. Scan for dates, ages, 'first/then/later/finally', and tense shifts (past perfect → simple past → present). These give the order directly with no logic required.

Do not read for meaning; read for LINKS. You can correctly order a paragraph about semiconductor fabrication without understanding semiconductors. Deliberately refusing to comprehend is faster and just as accurate.
If the set is presented with sentence 1 fixed and only P-Q-R-S to arrange, you are ordering four items, not five — treat it as pure pairing and it becomes a 45-second question.
When you are down to two options, compare only the position where they DIFFER. Do not re-read both full orders.
traps: Constructing the whole sequence from scratch instead of using the options to eliminate. This is the single biggest time sink in the English section and the reason para jumble sets get abandoned half-finished.
Assuming the most general sentence must be the opener. Sometimes the opener is a specific hook and the general statement is the conclusion.
Being fooled by a pronoun whose antecedent sits inside its OWN sentence — 'The bank said it would expand' contains 'it' but is perfectly capable of being the opener.
Marking an answer after finding one plausible order without eliminating anything. If you did not cross out at least two options, you guessed and the 0.25 penalty is live.
Spending time on the middle sentences. Opener, closer and one confirmed pair almost always determine the answer; the middle sorts itself out.

In 'which sentence is fourth' formats, answering from your mental order without checking that your order actually matches one of the offered options. Your order may be wrong in a way the options would have revealed.

Leading the section with a para jumble set. It feels all-or-nothing and it is slow; the questions are individually scoreable but the set should be attempted in the middle of your run, not at the start.

e-sent-rearr.whatItIs: Fragments of a SINGLE sentence, labelled A/B/C/D or P/Q/R/S, that must be assembled into one grammatical sentence. Distinct from para jumbles: here grammar decides the order, not logic, which makes it faster once you recognise the difference.
e-sent-rearr.coreMethod:
1. Identify the unit first. If the pieces are complete sentences, it is a para jumble and logic rules. If the pieces are fragments that cannot stand alone, it is sentence rearrangement and GRAMMAR rules. Making this call in the first three seconds changes your whole approach.
2. Locate the fragment holding the MAIN VERB together with its subject. That is the spine of the sentence.
3. Find the fragment that can legally START. It cannot begin with a relative pronoun (which / who / that / whose), cannot begin with a coordinating conjunction that requires a preceding clause (and / but / so / or), cannot begin with a preposition-dependent phrase needing a prior noun, and if capitalisation is printed, must carry the capital.
4. CHAIN BY GRAMMATICAL HOOKS — this is the actual technique and it is a jigsaw with visible tabs:
   - a fragment ENDING in a preposition (in, of, with, to, for) must be followed by a noun phrase
   - a fragment ENDING in an article (a, an, the) must be followed by a noun or adjective
   - a fragment ENDING in 'that / which / who' must be followed by a verb phrase
   - a fragment STARTING with an '-ing' form attaches to the clause containing its subject
   - a fragment ENDING in a comma attaches to a clause, not a fragment
   - a fragment containing the sentence's only full stop is last
5. Assemble by hooks, then verify subject-verb agreement at every join.
6. Cross-check against the options and eliminate. If three of five options share the same opening fragment, start from that fragment and only decide the tail.
tricks: Read the FIRST and LAST word of every fragment before you read anything else. Write them down if the paper allows. Dangling prepositions, articles and relative pronouns at fragment edges lock the order without any comprehension — this converts the question from reading to matching and typically halves the time.
Punctuation is a free hook. A fragment ending in a comma is subordinate; a fragment carrying the full stop is terminal; a fragment with a semicolon splits two independent clauses.
The longest fragment containing subject + verb + object is usually the main clause and sits either first or immediately after an introductory phrase. Anchor there.
Read only the JOINS, never the whole assembled sentence during solving. You need each junction to be grammatical; the global meaning takes care of itself. Save one full read for final confirmation.
If two options survive, compare only the single position where they differ rather than re-reading both complete orders.
traps: Treating it as a para jumble and hunting for logical flow. Grammar decides it, and logic-hunting doubles the time.
Choosing an order that joins smoothly but produces two main verbs with no conjunction between them — the result is grammatical-sounding rubble, not a sentence.
Ignoring printed capitalisation when it is shown; it hands you the opener free.
Not verifying that the finished sentence has one complete subject and one main verb. A common wrong answer is a well-glued fragment pile that is not a sentence at all.
Reading fragments for vocabulary. The answer lives at the fragment edges, not in the content words.
Confusing the labelling conventions — some papers fix the first and last portions and ask you to order only the middle. Read the instruction line before solving.

e-wordswap.whatItIs: A sentence with four bold words labelled A-D, two of which have been interchanged. You pick the pair to swap back. It is a pure collocation test disguised as comprehension, and it is topic-blind — you never need to know what the sentence is about.
e-wordswap.coreMethod:
1. Read the sentence once. Identify the bold word that produces the loudest nonsense — you almost always notice one immediately ('he viewed the guitar' when 'played' belongs there). That word is your ANCHOR.
2. Find the anchor's correct home. Scan the other three bold positions and ask 'which slot actually needs this word?' That question gives you the pair directly, without evaluating all the pairs.
3. CONFIRM BY PART OF SPEECH. Swapped words are nearly always the same part of speech as each other — noun with noun, verb with verb, adjective with adjective. If your candidate pair is a noun and a verb, you are probably wrong. This rule alone kills half the option list and costs two seconds.
4. Substitute the pair and read ONLY the two affected phrases, not the whole sentence. If both now collocate naturally with their neighbours, mark it.
5. If no word looks obviously wrong on the first read, go to the option list and test pairs that share a part of speech, starting with the pair whose two contexts are most similar.
6. Mark 'no interchange required' only after confirming all four bold words collocate with their immediate neighbours.
7. The moment you find one clean pair, STOP. Do not verify the others. IBPS builds exactly one correct interchange.
tricks: Check each bold word against the word IMMEDIATELY beside it, not against the sentence as a whole. Word swap is collocation: 'make a decision' / 'take a decision' / 'heavy traffic' / 'strong tea' / 'commit a crime' / 'pose a threat'. A bold word that does not pair with its neighbour is the misplaced one, and this local check is roughly four times faster than reading the sentence again.

Scan for the SHAPE-MATCHED pair before reading for meaning. Two bold words that are both abstract nouns, both '-ing' forms, or both comparative adjectives are prime swap candidates. You can often spot the pair in five seconds on shape alone and then confirm on meaning.

You do not need to understand the sentence's topic. Word swap questions on macroeconomics, marine ecology or constitutional law are exactly as solvable as ones about traffic. Never skip a word swap for unfamiliar subject matter — this is free marks that aspirants throw away out of intimidation.
If a bold word sits directly after 'a' or 'an', check sound agreement. A mismatched article exposes the misplaced word instantly and requires no vocabulary at all.
A and D swap as often as adjacent pairs do. Do not assume the misplaced words are near each other — the setter deliberately separates them because distance makes the nonsense harder to hear.
traps: Swapping the two words that are semantically related — two economics terms, two weather words — merely because they feel connected. Topical relatedness is not evidence of misplacement, and this is the most common wrong answer.
Trying to relocate three words. Exactly two move.
Re-reading the whole sentence three or four times. One full read plus one targeted collocation check is the entire budget.
Missing the 'no interchange required' option and forcing a swap because the format seems to demand one.
Assuming the bold words must be swapped in the order they appear.
Over-thinking a sentence on an unfamiliar topic. The topic is irrelevant to the method — if you are thinking about the subject matter, you have left the technique.
Reading the swapped version of the whole sentence to verify. Read only the two repaired phrases; full re-reading costs 10 seconds per question across a 5-question Mains block.
e-wordswap.timeTarget: 20-25 seconds per question in Prelims; 25-30 seconds in Mains where sentences are longer. A 5-question Mains block should close in 2 to 2.5 minutes.
e-wordswap.masteryCheck: You spot the misplaced word within 8 seconds of a single read, and complete 10 word-swap questions in 4 minutes with 9 correct — and for each you can name the collocation that was broken.

e-wordrearr.whatItIs: A sentence containing several blanks with a set of words labelled (A)-(E) to be placed into them. Questions ask which word occupies a given position, or for the correct sequence. It is solved entirely by grammatical slot-typing, not by meaning.
e-wordrearr.coreMethod:
1. Read the sentence frame — the FIXED text around the blanks. The fixed words, not the movable ones, determine the answer.
2. For each blank, read the word immediately before and immediately after it and write down the grammatical type that slot demands. This slot-typing is the entire method.
3. TYPE EACH MOVABLE WORD by its suffix, which takes about five seconds for all five: -tion / -ity / -ness / -ment / -ance = noun; -ate / -ise / -ify / -en = verb; -ous / -ful / -ive / -al / -ic / -able = adjective; -ly = adverb. Words without a telling suffix get typed by meaning.
4. Place the MOST RESTRICTED words first — a past participle, a preposition, an '-ly' adverb, a word that only fits one slot. Never start with a common noun; nouns fit many slots and starting there guarantees rework.
5. Two or three words will have exactly one legal slot each. Place those, then the remaining one or two fall out by elimination and are confirmed by meaning.
6. Verify subject-verb agreement across the completed sentence. A plural subject taking a singular verb means you have mis-slotted.
7. Answer only the position actually asked.
tricks: Fixed-text articles and prepositions are your strongest hooks and they cost nothing to read: a blank after 'the' needs a noun or adjective; after 'to' needs a base verb or a noun; after 'very' needs an adjective or adverb; after 'has/have/had' needs a past participle; after 'is/are being' needs a past participle.
Suffix-typing all five words before touching the sentence takes five seconds and eliminates most of the search space. Do it as a fixed opening move every time.

If the question asks only 'which word comes at position 3', you often do not need the full arrangement. Type the words, pin position 3 from its adjacent fixed text, and check against the options. This can halve the time on a 5-question set.

In a 5-question set built on the same sentence family, solve the arrangement ONCE properly and then answer all five positional questions from it. Aspirants routinely re-solve for each question and lose 90 seconds.
The tense marker in the fixed text (has / was / will be) determines which verb form goes where. Find it before placing any verb.
traps: Solving the entire sentence when only one position is asked. Read the question stem first.
Confusing this with word swap. Here ALL the labelled words move into blanks; in word swap only two move and there are no blanks. Diagnosing the format wrong costs the whole question.
Forgetting that '-ing' forms can be gerunds functioning as nouns ('swimming is healthy'), not verbs. Mistyping a gerund as a verb misroutes two words at once.
Skimming the fixed text. The movable words are the visible part of the puzzle but the fixed text holds the answer.
Placing the nouns first because they are easiest to understand. Nouns are the least constrained and must go last.
Not re-checking agreement after the final placement — the last word placed is the one most likely to break it.
e-wordrearr.timeTarget: 25-35 seconds per question; a 5-question set built on the same sentence in 2 to 2.5 minutes total once you stop re-solving per question.
e-wordrearr.masteryCheck: You can suffix-type all five movable words in under 10 seconds and place them correctly in under 30 seconds, on 8 of 10 questions — and on a 5-question set you solve the arrangement once and answer all five from it.

e-wordusage.whatItIs: One word is given and used in three separate sentences (I, II, III). You identify which sentences use it correctly. Almost always exactly one question in the paper — a fast mark or a slow trap depending entirely on whether you run the checks in the right order.
e-wordusage.coreMethod:
1. Establish the word's PART OF SPEECH in each sentence first, before considering meaning at all. The commonest error IBPS plants is a noun used as a verb or the reverse — advice/advise, practice/practise, effect/affect, licence/license. Check the slot, not the dictionary.
2. Check the word's FIXED PREPOSITION or collocation in each sentence. A right meaning with a wrong preposition is still wrong usage. Comprise takes no 'of'. Discuss takes no 'about'. Dispose takes 'of'. Bestow takes 'on/upon'. Deprive takes 'of'. Consist takes 'of'. Result takes 'in' or 'from' with different meanings.
3. Check SENSE. Many test words carry two or three legitimate senses and IBPS deploys a plausible fourth that the word does not actually have. Ask whether this specific sense exists, not whether the sentence sounds acceptable.
4. Record a yes/no verdict for each of the three sentences BEFORE reading the options. Deciding first and matching second prevents the options from steering you.
5. Match your three verdicts to the option list.
6. If you are unsure on exactly one sentence, read the options to find the DISCRIMINATOR — often only one sentence separates the surviving options, so spend your remaining seconds only on that sentence and ignore the settled ones.
tricks: Run the part-of-speech test first, always. It resolves the majority of word-usage questions in seconds and requires no vocabulary depth whatsoever — you are checking grammar, not knowledge.
If the same collocation appears in two of the three sentences, those two stand or fall together. Treat them as a single unit and you have reduced a three-way judgement to a two-way one.

Read the options before finalising all three sentences. Frequently two sentences are agreed across every option and only one is contested; identify the contested sentence and spend your time only there.

The words IBPS recycles here are common words with many senses, not rare words: bear, hold, run, draw, set, take, keep, address, table, board, subject, present, object, count, record, issue, charge, order, place, mark. Expect an everyday word doing an unfamiliar job.

If a sentence reads perfectly naturally on the first pass, it is almost certainly correct. Planted errors in this format are glaring once you look for the right thing — trust fluency here more than you would in phrase replacement.
traps: Deciding a sentence is wrong because it sounds formal or unfamiliar. Formal register is not error, and this is where most marks in this format are lost.
Judging on meaning alone and walking past a preposition violation.
Missing that the target word appears in a different FORM across the three sentences — 'bear' may show up as 'bore' or 'borne', and the inflection itself may be the planted error.
Marking 'all three are correct' as a default because checking three sentences feels expensive. It is genuinely correct sometimes, but only mark it after three verdicts, not instead of them.
Spending 60 or 90 seconds on a single-mark question. Cap it at 40 seconds and move — the opportunity cost inside a 20-minute clock is two fillers.
Assuming the given word's most familiar sense is the only one being tested. The question exists precisely because the word has several.

e-oddone.topicName: Odd one out and spelling error
e-oddone.whatItIs: Two related formats. The spelling/inappropriate-word type gives a sentence with four bold words and asks which is wrongly spelt or contextually wrong, with 'All Correct' as the fifth option. The odd-one-out type gives four or five statements sharing a context and asks which does not belong.
e-oddone.coreMethod:
SPELLING / INAPPROPRIATE WORD:
1. Scan the four bold words for SPELLING in isolation first, before reading the sentence at all. Spelling is recognised, not reasoned — this pass takes five seconds and often ends the question.
2. Check double letters first: accommodate, occurrence, embarrass, committee, harass, necessary. Then check -ence/-ance and -ible/-able endings. These two families cover most planted spelling errors.
3. If all four are correctly spelt, NOW read the sentence and check contextual appropriateness. This is where the format hides its real difficulty — a correctly spelt word can be entirely the wrong word.
4. For appropriateness, check part of speech first: advice/advise, practice/practise, effect/affect, principal/principle, complement/compliment, stationary/stationery, eminent/imminent, adapt/adopt, elicit/illicit, discreet/discrete, counsel/council, canvas/canvass, moral/morale, personal/personnel, loose/lose.
5. Only after both passes may you mark 'All Correct'.

ODD ONE OUT:
1. Read all statements and name the shared theme in three or four words.
2. The intruder typically shifts the SUBJECT ENTITY, shifts the time frame or tense, states an evaluation of the opposite sign, or is a general definition sitting among specific claims.
3. Apply the LINKAGE test, which is more reliable than theme-matching: the four belonging statements will chain into a paragraph through shared nouns, pronouns and connectors. The intruder links to none of them. Try to pair each statement with another — the one with no partner is the answer.
4. You are not looking for the statement that is wrong or that you disagree with. You are looking for the one that is about something else.
tricks: Do the four-word spelling scan before reading the sentence. Most aspirants read the sentence first and burn 10 seconds recovering information they did not need.

Memorise the recurring misspelling set — banks recycle it relentlessly: accommodation, occurrence, embarrass, harass, privilege, recommend, separate, definitely, maintenance, questionnaire, entrepreneur, liaison, bureaucracy, conscience, committee, necessary, occasion, achievement, receive, existence, government, independent, environment, restaurant, rhythm, colleague, foreign, immediately, beginning, successful, acknowledgement, consensus, millennium, supersede.
Memorise the confusable-pairs list — roughly 40 pairs cover almost everything IBPS asks in the 'inappropriate word' version, and this is where the harder marks in this format sit.
For odd one out, the fastest single test is: which statement has a different grammatical SUBJECT from the others? Scan subjects only. Fifteen seconds.

In odd one out, if two statements both look odd, the true intruder is the one that cannot be placed ANYWHERE in a valid ordering — the other one will fit somewhere. Try placing each and the answer resolves.
Tense-frame shift is a strong intruder signal: four statements in present tense and one in past narrative usually identifies itself.
traps: Marking 'All Correct' too readily. IBPS plants an error in roughly four out of five of these questions, so a high 'All Correct' rate means you are under-checking.
Checking spelling only and never running the appropriateness pass. The contextually-wrong-but-correctly-spelt word is the format's main weapon and it is invisible if you stop after the spelling scan.

Marking British spellings as errors. IBPS uses British conventions — colour, realise, programme, centre, labour, defence — and does NOT test the British/American difference as a mistake. Do not mark 'organise' wrong.
In odd one out, choosing the statement you disagree with, or the one that seems least important. Neither opinion nor importance is the criterion; only linkage is.
In odd one out, choosing the most general statement — general statements are frequently the topic sentence and belong.
Confusing odd-one-out with coherent-paragraph. In odd one out you only remove; in coherent paragraph you remove AND order. Read the stem.
Spending more than 20 seconds on a spelling question. It is the fastest question type in the paper and should be treated as such.
e-oddone.timeTarget: 15-20 seconds per spelling/inappropriate-word question — the fastest format in the English section. 35-45 seconds per odd-one-out question, which is a genuinely different animal.
e-oddone.masteryCheck: On 10 misspelt-word questions you score 9 in under 3 minutes, AND you can write out 30 of the standard confusable pairs (affect/effect type) from memory with both meanings — the memory test, not the quiz score, is the real check.

e-idioms.whatItIs: An idiom is given, either standalone or embedded in a sentence, and you choose its meaning — or an idiom appears as one of the options in a phrase replacement or fillers question. Low direct weightage at Clerk level, but idioms leak into several other formats.
e-idioms.coreMethod:
1. Do not attempt to memorise a thousand idioms. Learn the roughly 150 that bank exams recycle, grouped by theme — money and business, time and urgency, difficulty and failure, success, relationships, communication, secrecy. Thematic grouping roughly doubles retention over alphabetical lists.
2. When you meet an idiom you know, answer in five seconds and move. Recognition questions should not be reasoned.
3. When you meet one you do not know, decode in this order:
   (a) POLARITY. Read the surrounding sentence and decide whether the required meaning is positive or negative. Kill every option with the wrong sign — this typically removes three of five.
   (b) LITERAL IMAGE. What picture do the words paint, and what human situation does that picture suggest? 'Burn the midnight oil' pictures working by lamplight. The image is often a usable clue even when the idiom is unfamiliar.
   (c) GRAMMATICAL SLOT. An idiom functioning as a verb phrase needs an option that is a verb phrase. Options of the wrong shape are wrong.
4. Reject any option that is simply a literal restatement of the idiom's words. Idioms are non-literal by definition, so the literal option is always a distractor.
5. If two options share the correct polarity, choose the one whose INTENSITY matches the sentence.
6. Apply the guessing rule: with 0.25 negative marking, guess only if you have eliminated at least two options. Otherwise leave it — one idiom is not worth the variance.
tricks: Polarity-matching alone converts an unknown idiom into a 1-in-2 or 1-in-3 in about ten seconds. Read the sentence, decide the sign, strike the wrong-sign options. This is the single technique that makes unknown idioms answerable.
Learn idioms INSIDE example sentences, never as a bare two-column list. In the exam you will always meet them in context, and context-learnt idioms are retrieved far faster than list-learnt ones.

Business and money idioms are over-represented in bank exams — prioritise: in the red, make ends meet, cut corners, a tall order, call the shots, the ball is in your court, bite the bullet, on the back burner, get the axe, cash cow, tighten the belt, turn a blind eye, go the extra mile, in the same boat, beat around the bush, once in a blue moon, at the drop of a hat, hit the nail on the head, burn the midnight oil, steal someone's thunder, break the ice, keep at bay, on thin ice, a blessing in disguise, bring to the table.

If the idiom contains a body part or an animal, it is almost certainly in the standard recycled list. Recognise it or skip it within five seconds rather than reasoning about it — reasoning about a fixed expression you have simply never seen does not work.

Do idioms as spaced revision during dead time — commute, queues, before sleep — never as a dedicated 60-minute block. The weightage does not justify prime study hours, and memorisation works better distributed anyway.
traps: Choosing the literal meaning. This is the entire trap of the topic and the option is always present.

Confusing near-identical idioms: call it a day vs call it quits; on the cards vs in the cards; take for granted vs take for a ride; pull one's leg vs pull one's socks up; make up vs make out; put up with vs put up to.
Translating from a similar-sounding Hindi idiom. Several map to genuinely different meanings and the false-friend feels convincing.
Spending 60 seconds on a one-mark idiom you do not know. Polarity-eliminate, and either guess with two options gone or leave it.
Guessing blind. At 0.25 negative marking a blind five-way guess has an expected value of exactly zero — it adds variance and no marks.
Over-investing in this topic because idiom lists feel like productive studying. They are the most satisfying and least efficient English preparation available at Clerk level.
e-idioms.timeTarget: 15-20 seconds if you know it. If unknown: 20 seconds maximum to polarity-eliminate, then guess if two are gone or leave it. Never exceed 30 seconds.
e-idioms.masteryCheck: You can define 120 of the standard bank-exam idioms cold, tested by someone reading them aloud at random — and on an idiom you have never seen, you can eliminate at least two options by polarity within 10 seconds.

e-matchcol.whatItIs: Two columns of sentence fragments — Column I with items A, B, C and Column II with items D, E, F. You match them to form grammatically and contextually correct sentences. Crucially, not every item must find a partner: 'may or may not connect' is part of the standard instruction.
e-matchcol.coreMethod:
1. Read the instruction line. Confirm whether unmatched items are permitted — in the IBPS version they are, and assuming a complete one-to-one matching is the format's principal trap.
2. Do NOT test all nine combinations. Start from the item with the MOST grammatical constraint: the one ending in a preposition, a relative pronoun, an incomplete verb phrase, or a conjunction.
3. Read only the EDGES. For each Column I item, note the last two or three words. For each Column II item, note the first two or three words. You are matching junctions, not reading sentences — this is the difference between a 40-second question and a 90-second one.
4. Apply grammar filters at the junction, in this order: (a) subject-verb agreement across the join, (b) tense compatibility, (c) preposition or article completion, (d) number agreement of any pronoun crossing the join.
5. Then apply a two-second sense check. The completed sentence must be sensible, not merely legal — the standard distractor is a join that is grammatically flawless and semantically absurd.
6. USE THE OPTIONS TO CONSTRAIN. Find the ONE match you are most confident about and eliminate every option that does not contain it. Frequently a single confident match determines the whole answer without your evaluating the other two.
7. Answer the question actually asked — some sets ask only which single pairing is valid, not the full mapping.
tricks: Read only the junction words. The last three words of a Column I item and the first three of a Column II item contain everything that decides the match. Reading all six items in full costs 40 seconds you do not have inside a 20-minute clock.

The relative-pronoun test is the fastest single filter: if a Column I item ends with 'which', 'who' or 'that', the matching Column II item must begin with a VERB, not with a subject. This kills most candidates instantly.
Number agreement across the join: a Column I item ending in a plural noun demands a plural verb at the start of its partner. Scan for singular/plural mismatch before reading meaning at all.

Attack the option list first. If every option contains 'B-D', then B-D is free and you only have to decide A and C — you have converted a nine-combination problem into a four-combination one before doing any grammar.

When two candidate matches both work grammatically, the wrong one is nearly always the one that is semantically absurd rather than the one that is semantically dull. Correct matches in this format tend to produce ordinary, unremarkable sentences.
traps: Assuming a complete one-to-one matching. IBPS explicitly allows items to go unmatched, so 'only A-E' is a legal and frequently correct answer. Forcing three matches is the commonest way this question is lost.
Matching on topic similarity instead of grammar. Two halves about the same subject can be grammatically incapable of joining.
Reading all six items in full before starting. Junction-only reading is not a shortcut, it is the method.
Missing a subject-verb disagreement because the join falls mid-clause and the disagreement is not audible.
Not checking that the completed sentence contains exactly one main verb — a join can produce two main verbs with no conjunction and still sound acceptable at speed.
Solving all three matches when the question asks for only one valid pairing.
e-matchcol.timeTarget: 30-40 seconds per question when it is a 3-question set built on the same columns, so roughly 2 minutes for the whole set. Reading the columns is a fixed cost paid once — which is exactly why you must not re-read them for each question.
e-matchcol.masteryCheck: You complete a 3-item match-the-column set in under 2 minutes with all three correct, deciding every match on junction words alone — and you can state, for each rejected pairing, whether it failed on agreement, tense, preposition or sense.
